title: Production Kubernetes Cluster - Pods CrashLooping
description: Multiple pods across different namespaces are in CrashLoopBackOff state. Application services are intermittently unavailable.
symptoms: kubectl get pods shows CrashLoopBackOff status
Increased error rates in APM dashboard
logs: 10:01 payment-api Memory usage at 45.0%
10:05 payment-api Memory usage at 70.0% (WARN)
10:09 payment-api Memory usage at 90.0% (WARN, severity=high)
10:10 payment-api OOMKilled: Container exceeded memory limit (ERROR, severity=critical)
root_cause: PostgreSQL pod crashed due to OOMKilled (Out of Memory). The database pod had a memory limit of 2Gi but actual usage exceeded this during a batch job execution. When the database went down, all dependent application pods couldn't establish connections and entered CrashLoopBackOff.
resolution: Identified OOMKilled in database pod events: kubectl describe pod postgres-0 -n database
Immediately scaled up memory limit from 2Gi to 4Gi in the StatefulSet
Restarted the PostgreSQL pod to recover service
Application pods automatically recovered once database was accessible
preventive_actions: Implement proper resource requests and limits based on actual usage patterns
Set up proactive monitoring and alerting for memory utilization (alert at 80% threshold)
Configure Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) for application pods
Implement circuit breaker pattern in applications to handle database outages
impact: 15% of user requests failed during the 25-minute outage window
lesson_learned: Set memory limits from real usage data and alert at 80% before OOMKilled cascades to dependents.

title: CI/CD Pipeline Failing - Docker Build Timeout
description: Jenkins pipeline consistently failing at Docker build stage with timeout errors. Deployment to staging environment blocked.
symptoms: Docker build stage times out after 10 minutes
Error message: 'Step timed out after 10 minutes'
Build logs show slow package downloads
Pipeline success rate dropped from 95% to 20%
root_cause: The Jenkins agent's Docker network was using an outdated DNS resolver that was experiencing issues. npm package downloads were timing out due to DNS resolution failures and slow responses. The secondary DNS server was experiencing regional outages.
resolution: Updated Jenkins agent Docker daemon configuration
Modified /etc/docker/daemon.json to use primary DNS: 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8
Restarted Docker daemon: sudo systemctl restart docker
Cleared Docker build cache: docker builder prune -a -f
preventive_actions: Configure DNS monitoring for CI/CD infrastructure
Implement Docker layer caching to reduce dependency on external registries
Set up a private npm registry mirror for faster and more reliable builds
Add health checks for external dependencies before starting builds
impact: 12 deployments blocked, 3-hour delay in releasing critical bug fix
lesson_learned: CI/CD infrastructure needs DNS health monitoring just like production services do.

title: AWS Lambda Cold Start Causing Timeout
description: Lambda function handling user authentication experiencing frequent timeouts during cold starts, causing login failures.
symptoms: CloudWatch logs show cold start duration of 8-12 seconds
Error rate spike during low-traffic periods
root_cause: Lambda function had a bloated deployment package (245 MB) with unnecessary data science libraries (pandas, numpy, scipy) imported at the module level but only used by a separate analytics function. Cold starts required loading all of these into memory, causing 9-10 second init times.
resolution: Analyzed Lambda function code and identified unused dependencies
Removed pandas, numpy, and scipy from requirements.txt
Moved analytics logic to a separate Lambda function
Reduced deployment package from 245 MB to 15 MB
Evaluated Provisioned Concurrency for the auth function
preventive_actions: Implement dependency analysis in CI/CD pipeline to detect bloated packages
Use Lambda layers for shared dependencies
Set up alerts for cold start duration exceeding threshold
Regular audit of Lambda function dependencies
impact: Approximately 5% of login attempts failed during the incident window
lesson_learned: Audit Lambda deployment package size in CI; unused heavy dependencies directly cost cold-start latency.

title: Terraform Apply Fails - State Lock Acquisition
description: Terraform deployment stuck unable to acquire state lock. Infrastructure changes blocked.
symptoms: terraform apply hangs at 'Acquiring state lock'
Error: Error locking state: state already locked
Lock Info shows ID from 2 days ago
root_cause: A previous Jenkins pipeline job was terminated abruptly during a controller restart while running 'terraform apply'. The process didn't gracefully release the DynamoDB state lock, leaving a stale lock ID.
resolution: Verified no active Terraform processes in Jenkins or developer machines
Checked DynamoDB table for lock entry and confirmed it was stale (2 days old)
Backed up current Terraform state file from S3
Executed: terraform force-unlock <lock-id> after confirming safety
Successfully unlocked the state and re-ran apply
preventive_actions: Implement proper Jenkins job cleanup hooks to release locks on termination
Set up automated stale lock detection and alerts (locks older than 1 hour)
Configure Terraform state lock timeout to auto-release after 20 minutes
Use Jenkins shared libraries with proper error handling for Terraform operations
impact: Staging environment updates delayed by 1.5 hours, no production impact
lesson_learned: Terraform state locks must have an auto-release timeout so an abrupt job kill can't strand a lock indefinitely.

title: Nginx Ingress - SSL Certificate Renewal Failed
description: SSL certificate for production domain expired. Users seeing 'NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID' errors. Website inaccessible via HTTPS.
symptoms: Browser showing SSL certificate expired warning
Certificate valid until date shows 3 days ago
HTTPS traffic failing, HTTP redirects not working
root_cause: Let's Encrypt certificate auto-renewal failed because cert-manager couldn't complete the HTTP-01 ACME challenge. A recent WAF/firewall rule update blocked incoming traffic on port 80 to the ingress controller.
resolution: Immediately identified firewall rule blocking port 80 Let's Encrypt validation
Coordinated with security team to whitelist Let's Encrypt IP ranges
Updated WAF rules to allow traffic to .well-known/acme-challenge/* path
Manually triggered certificate renewal via cert-manager
preventive_actions: Implement alerting for certificate expiration (30, 15, and 7 days before)
Add automated tests for ACME challenge endpoint accessibility
Document Let's Encrypt IP ranges in security policies
Configure cert-manager to use DNS-01 challenge instead of HTTP-01
impact: Production website inaccessible for 50 minutes. Estimated 25,000 users affected.
lesson_learned: Certificate renewal paths (ACME challenges) must be explicitly allow-listed whenever WAF/firewall rules change.

title: Redis Cache Cluster - Memory Eviction Storm
description: Redis cluster experiencing massive cache evictions, causing database overload and application slowdown.
symptoms: Application response time increased from 200ms to 3000ms
Database CPU utilization jumped from 30% to 95%
Cache hit rate dropped from 95% to 40%
root_cause: A newly deployed analytics feature was storing uncompressed temporary computation results directly in Redis with long TTLs (24 hours), 5-10MB per request. Over 6 hours this filled Redis memory to capacity, triggering aggressive eviction of frequently-used session data.
resolution: Identified and immediately stopped the analytics service to prevent further memory pressure
Deleted analytics temporary keys via redis-cli SCAN + DEL
Reconfigured analytics service to use database temporary tables instead of Redis
preventive_actions: Implement Redis memory monitoring with alerts at 70%, 85%, and 95% thresholds
Establish Redis key naming conventions and TTL policies
Code review process must include cache storage impact analysis
Use separate Redis clusters for different data types (sessions, cache, temporary data)
impact: Application performance degraded for 1 hour 35 minutes. Slow response times affected all users. No data loss.
lesson_learned: New features that write to shared caches need a TTL and size review before launch, not after an eviction storm.

title: Docker Registry - Disk Space Exhaustion
description: Private Docker registry server out of disk space. Unable to push new container images, blocking all deployments.
symptoms: docker push failing with 'insufficient storage' error
All CI/CD pipelines failing at image push stage
root_cause: Docker registry had no garbage collection or cleanup policy implemented. Over 2 years of operation the registry accumulated thousands of outdated image versions (8,432 tags, 2TB), with most never cleaned up.
resolution: Immediately identified top 50 largest and oldest image repositories
Coordinated with dev teams to identify which images were safe to delete
Deleted all images older than 6 months with 'feature-*' and 'test-*' tags
Ran registry garbage collection: docker exec registry bin/registry garbage-collect
preventive_actions: Implement automated Docker registry garbage collection (daily/weekly schedule)
Enforce image retention policies based on tags and age
Set up disk space monitoring with alerts at 70% and 85% thresholds
Implement CI/CD pipeline image tagging standards (semantic versioning, branch names)
impact: All deployments blocked for 3 hours 45 minutes. 8 production releases delayed.
lesson_learned: Any registry/artifact store needs a retention policy from day one — 'we'll clean it up later' becomes 2TB.

title: Prometheus Monitoring - High Cardinality Causing OOM
description: Prometheus server repeatedly crashing due to out-of-memory errors. Monitoring and alerting system unavailable.
symptoms: Alerts not firing despite known issues
Prometheus memory usage growing to 32GB+ before crash
root_cause: A recently deployed application was instrumented with high-cardinality Prometheus labels (user_id, session_id, request_id) on http_requests_total. With 500,000+ unique users this created 8.5 million+ unique time series.
resolution: Identified problematic high-cardinality metrics using Prometheus TSDB status API
Immediately added metric_relabel_configs to drop high-cardinality labels
Removed user_id, session_id, and request_id labels from http_requests_total
Kept only necessary labels: method, status_code, endpoint_pattern
preventive_actions: Establish Prometheus metric instrumentation guidelines and review process
Implement cardinality limits and monitoring
Set up alerts for high cardinality metrics (>10k series per metric)
Use recording rules to pre-aggregate high-cardinality data
impact: Monitoring blind spot for 3 hours. Several alerts didn't fire during this period. No application downtime but reduced observability.
lesson_learned: Never let user-level identifiers (user_id, session_id) become metric labels; cardinality is a production risk.

title: Elasticsearch Cluster - Split Brain Scenario
description: Elasticsearch cluster split into two separate clusters, each believing itself to be primary. Data inconsistency and indexing failures occurring.
symptoms: Cluster health API showing different states from different nodes
logs: 13:20 redis-cluster-2 High latency to peer nodes: 100ms (WARN)
13:21 redis-cluster-2 High latency to peer nodes: 450ms (WARN)
13:22 redis-cluster-2 Network partition detected - unable to reach quorum (ERROR, severity=critical)
root_cause: Network partition caused by misconfigured Kubernetes NetworkPolicy blocked inter-node communication between two groups of Elasticsearch pods in different availability zones. minimum_master_nodes was also incorrectly set to 3 instead of the safe (N/2)+1 value for a 7-node cluster.
resolution: Immediately stopped all application writes to Elasticsearch to prevent further data inconsistency
Identified network partition cause - incorrect NetworkPolicy blocking AZ-to-AZ traffic
Corrected NetworkPolicy to allow Elasticsearch inter-node communication on ports 9200 and 9300
Shut down the minority-side nodes and let the cluster re-form around the majority
preventive_actions: Always set minimum_master_nodes to (N/2)+1 where N is total master-eligible nodes
Implement network monitoring between Elasticsearch nodes
Use discovery.seed_hosts and cluster.initial_master_nodes in Elasticsearch 7.x+
Test network policy changes in staging before production rollout
impact: Data inconsistency for 25 minutes. Search results were inconsistent. Some writes were duplicated or lost. Required manual data reconciliation post-incident.
lesson_learned: Quorum settings (minimum_master_nodes) must be validated against actual node count, not left at a default.

title: Kubernetes Pods Repeatedly OOMKilled Due to Memory Leak in Node.js Checkout Service
description: The checkout-service deployment in the payments namespace began experiencing repeated pod restarts as memory usage climbed steadily over several hours until pods exceeded their configured memory limits and were killed by the kubelet.
symptoms: kubectl describe pod showing reason OOMKilled
Gradual increase in memory usage visible in Grafana dashboards
Node memory pressure events in kubelet logs
logs: kubelet: Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 18422 (node) total-vm:2100000kB
kube-apiserver: Pod checkout-service-7d4b9c-xk2p9 status.phase=Failed reason=OOMKilled
app: [WARN] Heap usage at 1.8GB, approaching limit of 2Gi
app: [ERROR] FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
kube-scheduler: rescheduling pod checkout-service-7d4b9c-xk2p9 on node ip-10-0-4-12
kubelet: eviction manager: attempting to reclaim memory
root_cause: A memory leak was introduced in a recent release where event listeners on a shared EventEmitter were not being removed after each checkout request, causing retained references to request objects to accumulate over time until the container exceeded its memory limit.
resolution: Rolled back checkout-service deployment to previous stable image tag
Captured heap snapshot using node --inspect for offline analysis
Identified and patched the unbounded event listener registration in the order processing module
Increased memory limit temporarily from 2Gi to 3Gi as a safety buffer
Redeployed patched image and monitored memory usage for 24 hours
Verified garbage collection behavior returned to expected sawtooth pattern
preventive_actions: Add heap usage alerting at 70 percent of container memory limit
Introduce automated memory leak detection in CI using clinic.js
Mandate code review checklist item for event listener cleanup
Set up periodic node --prof profiling in staging under load testing
Add Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendation mode for early detection
Document incident in postmortem wiki with heap snapshot analysis steps
impact: Checkout functionality was degraded intermittently for approximately 90 minutes, resulting in an estimated 4 percent drop in successful checkout completions during the incident window.
lesson_learned: Memory growth trends should be tracked over multi-hour windows rather than relying solely on instantaneous alerts, since gradual leaks can evade threshold-based alerting until the final crash.

title: Docker Image Pull Failures Across Fleet Due to Expired Private Registry Credentials
description: New pod deployments and node autoscaling events across multiple clusters began failing because the imagePullSecret used to authenticate with the private Harbor registry had expired, blocking all new container image pulls.
symptoms: ErrImagePull events in kubectl describe output
New node joins failing to pull base images
Deployment rollouts stalling with zero available replicas
Autoscaler scaling up nodes that never became ready

harbor-core: token expired at 2025-01-17T00:00:00Z rejecting request
kubelet: back-off pulling image registry.internal/app:1.42
root_cause: The Kubernetes imagePullSecret was created from a Harbor robot account token that had a 90 day expiration policy, and no automated rotation or expiry alerting existed, so the credential silently expired without renewal.
resolution: Generated a new long-lived Harbor robot account token
Recreated the imagePullSecret in all affected namespaces using kubectl create secret docker-registry
Patched default service accounts to reference the updated secret
Manually triggered rollout restart on stuck deployments
Verified new node joins could pull images successfully
Cordoned and drained nodes stuck in NotReady due to failed image pulls
preventive_actions: Automate robot account token rotation via a scheduled CronJob
Add Prometheus alert 30 days before token expiration
Store registry credentials in Vault with automatic secret injection
Mirror critical base images to a secondary registry for redundancy
Add a synthetic canary pod deployment to detect pull failures early
Document credential ownership and rotation runbook
impact: Approximately 22 deployments across three clusters were unable to roll out new versions or scale for 2 hours, and 6 nodes failed to join their clusters during the window.
lesson_learned: Long-lived credentials without expiry monitoring are a silent single point of failure; any secret with a fixed TTL needs an automated alert well before expiration.

description: Multiple Jenkins build agents began failing jobs with workspace write errors after accumulated build artifacts and Docker layer caches filled the local disk to capacity.

Docker build steps failing to write image layers
Slow build times before eventual failure

systemd: docker.service: Failed with result exit-code
root_cause: Automated cleanup jobs for old Docker images and Jenkins workspace artifacts had been disabled during a previous maintenance window and never re-enabled, allowing disk usage to grow unchecked over several weeks.
resolution: Identified affected agents via disk usage dashboard
Manually ran docker system prune -a on all affected agents
Cleared old Jenkins workspace directories older than 14 days
Re-enabled the scheduled cleanup CronJob that had been disabled
Restarted Docker daemon and reconnected Jenkins agents
Reran failed pipeline builds to confirm resolution
preventive_actions: Add disk usage alerting at 75 percent threshold per agent
Implement automatic docker system prune as a nightly scheduled task
Add workspace retention policy directly in Jenkinsfile using cleanWs
Move build artifact storage to a dedicated larger EBS volume
Add a pre-flight disk space check step before each pipeline run
Include disabled maintenance task check in weekly ops review
impact: Roughly 40 CI pipeline runs failed or were delayed over a 3 hour period, delaying two planned production deployments.
lesson_learned: Temporary changes made during maintenance windows must be tracked and reverted with an explicit checklist, since silently disabled automation can cause slow-building failures that are hard to trace.

Manually killed the orphaned process holding the lock
Removed the stale .lock file from the workspace
Re-triggered the nightly release pipeline manually
Verified the pipeline completed successfully end to end

Configure agents to clean workspace locks on abnormal restart
Add pipeline stage timeouts to prevent indefinite hangs
Move to ephemeral, containerized Jenkins agents per build
Add alerting for builds running longer than expected duration

lesson_learned: Long-lived, non-ephemeral build agents accumulate state issues over time; moving to ephemeral per-build agents eliminates entire classes of stale-lock and workspace-corruption incidents.

Add automated connectivity health check pinging api.github.com every 5 minutes

title: Terraform Apply Blocked Indefinitely Due to Stale State Lock in DynamoDB
description: All terraform apply and plan operations across the infrastructure repository began failing with a state lock error after a previous CI job was forcibly terminated mid-apply, leaving a stale lock record in the DynamoDB lock table.
symptoms: terraform plan failing immediately with Error acquiring the state lock
CI pipeline stuck waiting on lock acquisition timeout
Engineers unable to run any infrastructure changes
DynamoDB table showing a lock entry with an old timestamp
No active terraform process actually holding the lock

root_cause: A Jenkins job running terraform apply was killed after exceeding its build timeout while mid-apply, and because the lock release is handled by a SIGTERM/defer in the Terraform CLI, the abrupt kill signal (SIGKILL from Jenkins timeout policy) prevented the lock from being released in DynamoDB.
resolution: Verified no terraform process was actually running against the state file
Confirmed via S3 object version history that the state file was not mid-write
Ran terraform force-unlock with the lock ID from the error message
Re-ran terraform plan to confirm state consistency
Applied the originally intended infrastructure change successfully
Reviewed Jenkins job timeout settings to prevent future abrupt kills
preventive_actions: Increase Jenkins build timeout for terraform apply stages to accommodate large changesets
Configure Jenkins to send SIGTERM with a grace period before SIGKILL
Add automated stale lock detection and alerting after 30 minutes
Split large terraform applies into smaller targeted applies
Add terraform plan output review gate before apply to reduce apply duration
Document force-unlock procedure with required verification steps in runbook
impact: Infrastructure changes were blocked for 45 minutes, delaying a scheduled network ACL update and a new RDS instance provisioning task.
lesson_learned: CI job termination policies must account for tools like Terraform that require graceful shutdown to release distributed locks; abrupt kills can leave infrastructure automation blocked even when no real conflict exists.

title: Ansible Playbook Failure Across Fleet Due to Rotated SSH Host Keys
description: A scheduled Ansible playbook run for applying security patches across the production fleet failed on the majority of hosts after a recent host key rotation invalidated the known_hosts entries cached by the Ansible control node.
symptoms: Playbook runs failing with host key verification failed errors
SSH connection refused messages in verbose Ansible output
Patch compliance dashboard showing dropping coverage percentage
Manual ssh from control node also failing with the same host key warning
logs: ansible: fatal: [web-prod-14]: UNREACHABLE! => host key verification failed
ansible: WARNING REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED

ansible-playbook: PLAY RECAP: web-prod-14 : unreachable=1
cron: ansible-playbook exited with return code 4
root_cause: A separate security initiative had rotated SSH host keys on all production servers as part of a hardening effort, but the change did not include updating the Ansible control node's known_hosts cache or configuring StrictHostKeyChecking appropriately, causing Ansible to reject connections to hosts with new keys.
resolution: Confirmed the host key rotation was an intentional, authorized security change
Removed stale entries from known_hosts using ssh-keygen -R for affected hosts
Used ansible-playbook with a one-time ssh-keyscan refresh task to repopulate known_hosts
Verified connectivity to all hosts using ansible all -m ping
Re-ran the delayed security patch playbook successfully
Coordinated with the security team on future host key rotation notifications
preventive_actions: Add automated known_hosts refresh step triggered by host key rotation events
Integrate host key management with a centralized SSH CA to avoid manual known_hosts updates
Require cross-team notification process for any host key or credential rotation affecting automation
Add pre-flight connectivity check step before scheduled playbook runs
Store known_hosts centrally in version control with automated sync
Add alerting when patch compliance percentage drops below threshold
impact: Automated security patching was delayed by approximately 2 hours across 85 percent of the production fleet, temporarily reducing patch compliance reporting accuracy.
lesson_learned: Security hardening initiatives like host key rotation must be coordinated with configuration management tooling ownership, since infrastructure automation often has implicit trust dependencies that are easy to overlook.

description: A scheduled Ansible playbook run to deploy configuration updates across the application server fleet failed on roughly 60% of hosts with SSH authentication errors.

Confirmed the bootstrap automation referenced the old key fingerprint
Updated the bootstrap template to reference the current public key

Store the deploy public key reference in a single source of truth
Add automated tests for the host bootstrap process on new AMI builds

impact: 63 application servers missed scheduled configuration updates for approximately 50 minutes, and several accumulated config drift requiring manual remediation.
lesson_learned: Credential rotations must be propagated to every automation path that references them, including provisioning and bootstrap pipelines, not just the primary configuration management tool.

title: ECS Task Placement Failures Due to Insufficient CPU Reservation on Cluster
description: New deployments of the recommendation-engine ECS service failed to place tasks after a configuration change increased the CPU reservation per task without a corresponding increase in cluster capacity, leaving insufficient resources across all container instances.
symptoms: ECS service events showing unable to place task because no container instance met all requirements
Desired task count not being reached
Existing tasks running fine while new ones failed to start
Cluster CPU reservation shown near 100 percent in ECS console
Deployment stuck in IN_PROGRESS state indefinitely

ecs: Deployment recommendation-engine-deploy-2025-02-06 rolloutState IN_PROGRESS
autoscaling: capacity provider unable to scale out, at maximum instance count
root_cause: A task definition update doubled the CPU reservation per task from 512 to 1024 CPU units as part of a performance tuning change, but the underlying EC2 Auto Scaling Group backing the ECS capacity provider was already near its maximum instance count, leaving no room for the scheduler to place the larger tasks.
resolution: Identified the CPU reservation increase in the recent task definition revision
Temporarily increased the Auto Scaling Group maximum instance count
Triggered capacity provider scale-out to add additional container instances
Verified new tasks placed successfully once capacity was available
Confirmed desired task count reached and old tasks drained
Reviewed capacity planning to align with the new resource requirements
preventive_actions: Add automated capacity planning check comparing task resource requirements against cluster headroom before deployment
Set ECS capacity provider managed scaling target tracking at a lower utilization threshold
Add CloudWatch alarm for ClusterCPUReservation exceeding 85 percent
Require infrastructure capacity review as part of task definition CPU or memory changes
Use Fargate for services with variable resource requirements to avoid capacity constraints
Document task sizing change process requiring capacity sign-off
impact: The recommendation-engine deployment was stuck for 50 minutes, though existing production traffic continued to be served by already-running tasks with no customer-facing downtime.
lesson_learned: Task-level resource requirement changes must be reviewed against cluster capacity headroom before deployment, since ECS will not proactively warn that a routine task definition change could outstrip available cluster resources.

title: EC2 Instances Unreachable After Security Group Automation Error
description: A batch of EC2 instances behind the internal API load balancer became completely unreachable over SSH and HTTP shortly after an automated security group cleanup script ran.
symptoms: SSH connections timing out to all affected instances
Health checks on the internal load balancer failing for the same instances
No recent application-level deployments to those instances
AWS Config showing recent security group rule changes
Traffic completely dropped rather than refused

resolution: Identified the security group rule changes via AWS Config change history
Disabled the automated cleanup Lambda to prevent further changes
Manually restored the removed inbound rules for ports 443 and 22
Verified load balancer health checks returned to healthy
Audited other security groups for similar recent unwanted changes
preventive_actions: Require manual approval before the cleanup Lambda applies changes
Extend the traffic lookback window used to determine rule usage
Add security groups attached to load balancers to a protected exclusion list
Add automated rollback capability for security group changes
Add alerting on any security group rule removal in production VPCs
impact: The internal API was completely unreachable for approximately 18 minutes, affecting all downstream services that depend on it, including order processing.
lesson_learned: Automated cleanup tooling touching network security controls needs conservative safeguards such as approval gates and protected resource exclusions, since false positives can cause immediate, total outages.

title: EKS Node Group Autoscaling Failure Due to Missing IAM Trust Policy Update
description: During a traffic surge, the Cluster Autoscaler attempted to scale out an EKS managed node group but new nodes failed to join the cluster because the node instance role's trust policy had not been updated after a recent AWS account IAM boundary migration.
symptoms: Pods stuck in Pending state despite autoscaler triggering scale-out
New EC2 instances launching but never reaching Ready status
kubelet unable to register node with the API server
IAM AssumeRole errors visible in EC2 instance system logs

resolution: Compared the node instance role trust policy against a known-good backup from before the migration
Identified the missing trust relationship for the EKS service principal
Updated the IAM role trust policy to restore the correct assume role permissions
Terminated the stuck instances to force clean relaunch attempts
Verified new nodes successfully joined the cluster and pods scheduled
Confirmed autoscaler stabilized at the target node count
preventive_actions: Add IAM policy diff automation to the account migration change process
Create a test suite that validates all critical role trust policies after IAM migrations
Add CloudWatch alarm for nodes remaining NotReady beyond 5 minutes
Maintain infrastructure as code definitions for all node instance roles under version control
Add a synthetic node scale-out test in staging after any IAM-related change
Document EKS node bootstrap IAM dependencies in the platform runbook
impact: Autoscaling was ineffective for 40 minutes during a traffic surge, causing elevated latency and a small number of request timeouts on the affected service before manual intervention restored node capacity.
lesson_learned: IAM migrations that touch trust policies must include validation against all infrastructure-critical roles, since a missed role like the EKS node instance role can silently break autoscaling without any obvious error until a capacity event occurs.

title: Extended Application Downtime During Unplanned RDS Multi-AZ Failover
description: An underlying hardware fault on the primary RDS PostgreSQL instance triggered an automatic Multi-AZ failover to the standby replica, but application connection pools did not recover promptly because DNS caching at the connection pooler level prevented clients from picking up the new endpoint quickly.
symptoms: Sudden spike in database connection errors across all application services
RDS console showing failover event in progress
Application health checks failing with connection refused
PgBouncer logs showing repeated failed connection attempts to the old primary IP
Read replica lag briefly spiking during promotion
logs: rds: Multi-AZ instance failover started
rds: Multi-AZ instance failover completed, new primary is orders-db-instance-2
pgbouncer: ERROR could not connect to server: Connection refused, old-primary-ip:5432
app: [ERROR] FATAL: terminating connection due to administrator command
pgbouncer: server_idle_timeout, closing stale connections
cloudwatch: DatabaseConnections dropped from 480 to 0 then recovered to 460
root_cause: PgBouncer was configured with a DNS resolution cache TTL of 300 seconds, which was longer than the typical RDS failover completion time, causing connection pools to keep attempting connections to the old primary's cached IP address for several minutes after the failover had already completed and the endpoint's DNS record had updated.
resolution: Confirmed the Multi-AZ failover had completed successfully at the RDS level
Manually restarted PgBouncer instances to force DNS re-resolution
Verified application connections re-established to the new primary
Monitored replica lag and confirmed it returned to normal within minutes
Reviewed CloudWatch metrics to confirm full recovery of connection counts
Communicated incident timeline to affected service owners
preventive_actions: Reduce PgBouncer DNS cache TTL to 30 seconds or less
Implement RDS event subscription to automatically trigger pooler restarts on failover events
Use RDS Proxy to abstract failover handling away from application connection pools
Add synthetic database connectivity canary to detect failover recovery time
Conduct regular failover drills in a staging environment to validate recovery procedures
Document expected RTO for Multi-AZ failovers and validate against actual incident data
impact: Approximately 12 minutes of significant service degradation with elevated error rates across all services dependent on the orders database, affecting order placement and inventory checks.
lesson_learned: Database failover automation at the infrastructure level does not guarantee fast application-level recovery; connection pooling layers must be explicitly tuned or event-driven to avoid becoming the actual bottleneck during a failover.

title: Service-to-Service Authentication Outage After Overly Restrictive IAM Policy Deployment
description: A security tightening initiative deployed a new IAM policy restricting S3 access by source VPC endpoint, which inadvertently blocked the inventory-service from reading configuration files it depended on from a shared S3 bucket, causing the service to fail health checks.
symptoms: Inventory service pods failing readiness probes
Application logs showing AccessDenied errors reading from S3
Service reporting configuration not loaded on startup
CloudTrail showing a spike in S3 GetObject AccessDenied events

kubelet: Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode 503

root_cause: The new bucket policy required S3 access to originate from a specific VPC endpoint ID, but the inventory-service ran in a different subnet that used a separate, newer VPC endpoint which had not been included in the policy's allowed endpoint list, since the security team's audit had missed that subnet during discovery.
resolution: Reviewed CloudTrail logs to identify the specific denied requests and source VPC endpoint
Confirmed with the security team that the endpoint was legitimate but missing from policy
Updated the S3 bucket policy to include the additional VPC endpoint ID
Restarted inventory-service pods to retry configuration loading
Verified successful config load and passing readiness probes
Confirmed downstream services recovered automatically once inventory-service stabilized
preventive_actions: Require a comprehensive VPC endpoint inventory before deploying source-restricted IAM policies
Add a staged rollout process for IAM policy changes affecting production data access
Implement automated testing of S3 access from all known application subnets before policy activation
Add CloudTrail-based alerting for spikes in AccessDenied events immediately after policy changes
Maintain an IAM policy change calendar with rollback plans documented in advance
Add cross-team review requirement for any policy affecting shared, multi-consumer resources

title: Static Asset Delivery Outage Due to Accidental S3 Bucket Policy Overwrite
description: A Terraform apply intended to update logging configuration on the static assets S3 bucket inadvertently replaced the entire bucket policy document because the resource was defined with a full policy override rather than a merge, removing the public read permissions required for direct asset access.
symptoms: Website images and static files returning HTTP 403 Forbidden
CloudFront origin fetch failures logged as AccessDenied
Customer reports of broken images across the marketing site
S3 access logs showing a spike in 403 responses
No changes detected in application code or CloudFront configuration
logs: s3: AccessDenied Access Denied for object assets/logo.png
cloudfront: Origin returned HTTP status code 403
terraform: aws_s3_bucket_policy.assets: Modifying...
terraform: aws_s3_bucket_policy.assets: Modifications complete after 2s
cloudtrail: eventName PutBucketPolicy requestParameters bucketName cdn-assets-prod
s3-access-log: 403 GET /assets/logo.png
root_cause: The Terraform resource aws_s3_bucket_policy was defined using a policy document data source that only included logging-related statements, and applying it replaced the previously existing public read statement rather than appending to it, since S3 bucket policies are fully replaced on each PutBucketPolicy call rather than merged.
resolution: Identified the recent PutBucketPolicy event in CloudTrail as the trigger
Retrieved the previous bucket policy version from Terraform state history
Reconstructed a combined policy document including both logging and public read statements
Applied the corrected policy via terraform apply
Verified asset access restored by testing several public object URLs
Invalidated the CloudFront cache for the affected paths to clear cached 403 responses
preventive_actions: Always compose bucket policies as a single combined document with all required statements in Terraform
Add a terraform plan review step specifically flagging full resource replacements on IAM and bucket policy resources
Enable S3 bucket policy change notifications via CloudTrail and EventBridge
Add automated synthetic checks that verify public asset accessibility after any bucket policy change
Store previous bucket policy documents in version control with clear diffs for review
Add a pre-apply confirmation step for any change touching public-facing bucket policies
impact: Static assets were inaccessible for approximately 20 minutes, causing broken images and degraded page rendering across the public marketing website.
lesson_learned: S3 bucket policies are always fully replaced rather than merged, so infrastructure as code changes must always compose the complete intended policy rather than assuming incremental additions will be layered onto existing statements.

title: Site-Wide Outage After Route53 DNS Record TTL Misconfiguration During Failover
description: During a planned failover of the primary application load balancer to a disaster recovery region, a previously configured excessively long DNS TTL of 24 hours caused a large portion of global traffic to continue resolving to the decommissioned primary region's load balancer for many hours after the record was updated.
symptoms: Users in multiple regions unable to reach the application after DR cutover
Some users successfully reaching the new region while others still hit the old one
CloudWatch showing zero traffic on new ALB despite DNS record being updated
Old region's decommissioned ALB showing unexpected residual traffic
Support tickets from users describing intermittent access depending on network provider
Health check correctly marks primary region endpoint as unhealthy
Route53 correctly fails over the record set
Significant traffic volume still hitting the failed region per origin logs
Client-side DNS caches show the old IP address long after failover
logs: route53: Changed resource record set app.example.com from ALIAS old-alb to ALIAS new-alb
route53: TTL value 86400 on record app.example.com
alb-old: Target group has 0 registered healthy targets, still receiving requests
alb-new: RequestCount increasing gradually over several hours
resolver-logs: Cached response returned for app.example.com, TTL remaining 68000s
cloudwatch: 5xx error rate elevated for clients hitting decommissioned ALB
20:15:00 route53-healthcheck Endpoint us-east-1 marked Unhealthy
20:15:05 route53 Failover record set updated: primary -> secondary (us-west-2)
20:16:00 origin-logs us-east-1 still receiving 45% of expected traffic
21:20:00 origin-logs us-east-1 traffic finally dropping toward zero
affected_components: Route53 hosted zone record for app.example.com
root_cause: The DNS record's TTL had been set to 86400 seconds during initial setup and never revisited before the disaster recovery runbook was executed, meaning that despite the Route53 record being updated correctly, recursive resolvers around the world that had already cached the old record continued serving the previous ALB address for up to 24 hours.
resolution: Confirmed the Route53 record change had propagated correctly at the authoritative level
Identified the long TTL as the cause of delayed global propagation
Temporarily restored minimal capacity on the old region's ALB and target group to serve stale-cached traffic safely
Waited out the TTL expiration window while monitoring traffic shift
Once traffic fully shifted, decommissioned the old region's resources
Documented the incident timeline and traffic migration curve for postmortem
Confirmed Route53 had correctly updated the record set immediately upon failover
Identified the misconfigured 24-hour TTL as the cause of the propagation delay
Updated the TTL to 60 seconds for immediate effect on future changes
Manually restored partial capacity in the primary region as a mitigation while DNS caches expired naturally
Monitored traffic split until it fully shifted to the healthy region
preventive_actions: Reduce TTL to 60 seconds on all failover-critical DNS records well in advance of any planned cutover
Update the DR runbook to include a TTL reduction step at least 48 hours before any planned failover
Use Route53 health check based failover routing instead of manual record updates where possible
Add automated DNS propagation verification using multiple public resolvers before decommissioning old resources
Add monitoring dashboard showing traffic split between regions during any migration
Conduct quarterly DR failover drills that include DNS TTL validation as an explicit checklist item
Set DNS TTLs on all failover-critical records to 60 seconds or lower
Add TTL configuration checks to infrastructure review checklists for any DNS-dependent failover design
Document that Route53 health check speed does not equal client-side failover speed when TTL is high
Consider client-side retry/multi-endpoint logic as a faster failover mechanism than relying solely on DNS
impact: A significant portion of global users experienced intermittent or complete inability to access the application for up to 14 hours until DNS caches fully expired worldwide.
lesson_learned: DNS TTL values must be treated as a critical parameter of any failover plan and reduced well ahead of time, since even a correctly updated authoritative record cannot override resolvers that have already cached a long-TTL response.

title: EKS Cluster Autoscaler Stopped Scaling After IAM Policy Update
description: During a traffic surge, new pods remained in Pending state for over 15 minutes because the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler failed to launch additional worker nodes despite available capacity in the node group.

resolution: Reviewed cluster-autoscaler logs and identified the AccessDenied error
Compared the current IAM policy against the previous known-good version
Added the required permission back to the IAM policy with least-privilege scoping
Verified the autoscaler successfully scaled the ASG
Confirmed pending pods scheduled once new nodes joined the cluster
preventive_actions: Add IAM policy diff review as a required step for security hardening changes
Add integration tests that validate autoscaler permissions after IAM changes
Add alerting on cluster-autoscaler AccessDenied errors
Add alerting on sustained Pending pod counts exceeding a threshold
Maintain a documented least-privilege policy baseline for platform IAM roles
impact: Application capacity was constrained for approximately 15 minutes during a traffic surge, resulting in elevated latency and a small number of request timeouts.
lesson_learned: IAM least-privilege hardening changes need validation against the actual permissions required by platform automation like the Cluster Autoscaler, since removing seemingly broad permissions can silently break critical scaling functionality.

title: Cache Stampede and Latency Spike After Redis Maxmemory Eviction Storm
description: The Redis cluster backing the session cache began aggressively evicting keys under the allkeys-lru policy after memory usage hit the maxmemory limit, triggering a cache stampede as thousands of clients simultaneously fell back to the origin database for session lookups.
symptoms: Sharp increase in Redis evicted_keys metric
Application latency spiking as cache hit ratio dropped below 40 percent
Origin PostgreSQL database CPU usage climbing rapidly
Redis INFO memory showing used_memory at maxmemory limit continuously
Increased connection count on the database from cache-miss fallback queries
logs: redis: # WARNING Maxmemory reached, evicting keys
redis-cli: used_memory_human:5.98G maxmemory_human:6.00G
redis: evicted_keys 184320 (cumulative)
app: [WARN] Cache miss for session key, falling back to database
postgres: LOG: duration: 820.442 ms statement: SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE id = $1
redis: keyspace_misses 2891004
root_cause: A recent feature launch increased average session object size significantly by embedding additional user preference data, and without a corresponding increase to the Redis cluster's maxmemory setting, the larger objects caused the cluster to reach its memory ceiling much sooner than capacity planning had anticipated, triggering continuous eviction under load.
resolution: Identified the increased average session object size as the proximate cause via redis-cli --bigkeys sampling
Temporarily increased maxmemory on the Redis cluster nodes
Added TTL-based expiration to reduce retention of stale session data
Monitored cache hit ratio recovery back above 90 percent
Verified database CPU usage returned to baseline
Reviewed the feature launch's data model with the owning team
preventive_actions: Capacity plan Redis maxmemory based on projected object size growth ahead of feature launches
Add alerting when evicted_keys rate exceeds a defined threshold per minute
Reduce session object size by storing only session identifiers with detailed preferences in a separate store
Implement request coalescing or a mutex pattern to prevent cache stampede on concurrent misses
Add cache hit ratio to the standard service health dashboard
Require data model size review for any change to cached object schemas
impact: Session lookup latency increased by 3 to 5x for approximately 35 minutes, and database load reached 85 percent CPU utilization, degrading overall application responsiveness.
lesson_learned: Changes to the size of frequently cached objects must be capacity planned with the same rigor as traffic volume changes, since object size growth can silently erode effective cache capacity well before any traffic increase would.

title: Stale Read Data Served to Users Due to PostgreSQL Streaming Replication Lag
description: The reporting-api, which reads exclusively from a PostgreSQL streaming replica to offload the primary, began serving significantly outdated data after replication lag grew to over 20 minutes due to a long-running vacuum operation contending for I/O on the replica.
symptoms: Customer reports of reports showing data from over an hour ago
pg_stat_replication showing increasing replay_lag on the replica
Replica CPU and disk I/O utilization elevated
Application-level cache showing correct data while direct replica queries were stale

root_cause: An autovacuum operation on a large, heavily updated events table triggered on the replica coincided with a period of high read traffic, and because the replica's I/O capacity was already near saturation from routine query load, WAL replay fell significantly behind the primary, causing queries against the replica to return stale results without any error being surfaced to callers.
resolution: Confirmed replication lag via pg_stat_replication on the primary
Identified the concurrent autovacuum operation as the I/O contention source
Temporarily redirected reporting-api traffic to the primary to serve fresh data
Allowed the autovacuum operation to complete without interruption to avoid table bloat
Monitored replay_lag until it returned to sub-second levels
Redirected traffic back to the replica once lag normalized
preventive_actions: Tune autovacuum cost-based delay settings to reduce I/O impact during peak hours
Schedule aggressive vacuum operations during known low-traffic maintenance windows
Add explicit replication lag monitoring with alerting above a 30 second threshold
Include replica staleness indicator in API responses so clients can detect stale reads
Provision replica storage with higher IOPS to reduce contention risk
Consider a dedicated replica exclusively for analytical or reporting queries
impact: Reporting data was stale by up to 22 minutes for approximately 40 minutes, affecting business intelligence dashboards used by internal stakeholders with no direct customer-facing impact.
lesson_learned: Replication lag can be silent and undetected by application logic that assumes replicas are always near real-time; systems relying on replicas for reads need explicit lag monitoring and a defined fallback strategy.

title: S3 Bucket Policy Change Blocks Static Asset Delivery Site-Wide

resolution: Correlated the onset of errors with the timestamp of the bucket policy change
Reviewed the S3 bucket policy version history
Identified the removed statement as the CloudFront OAI grant
Reverted the bucket policy to the previous working version
Confirmed CloudFront successfully retrieved objects again
Verified the site rendered correctly for a sample of pages
preventive_actions: Require peer review with a diff summary for all S3 bucket policy changes
Add automated synthetic checks that validate static asset delivery after policy changes
Replace broad public-read statements with explicit, well-documented OAI-only access
Add a canary alert for CDN 4xx error rate spikes
Maintain an inventory of bucket policy statements with purpose annotations
impact: The website was effectively unusable, with all styling, images, and scripts failing to load for every visitor for approximately 9 minutes.
lesson_learned: Security remediation of S3 bucket policies must clearly distinguish between genuinely overly-broad public access and the specific principal grants required by legitimate infrastructure like CloudFront OAI, since removing the wrong statement causes an immediate total outage.

title: Order Processing Delays Due to MySQL Deadlock Storm During Peak Traffic
description: During a peak sales period, the order-processing service began experiencing a surge of MySQL deadlock errors as concurrent transactions updated the same set of inventory rows in inconsistent orders, causing a large percentage of order submissions to fail and retry.
symptoms: Elevated ER_LOCK_DEADLOCK errors in application logs
Order submission success rate dropping to 60 percent
InnoDB deadlock count metric climbing sharply
Retry storms amplifying overall database load
logs: mysql: ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
innodb: transaction 4029182 rolled back due to deadlock
app: [WARN] Retrying order submission after deadlock, attempt 2
mysql: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS: LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
app: [ERROR] Order submission failed after 3 retries for order_id 88213
mysql: Innodb_deadlocks counter incremented to 342
root_cause: The order submission code updated the inventory table and the order_items table in different orders depending on the code path taken, so under high concurrency, transactions acquiring row locks in opposite sequences frequently formed circular wait conditions that InnoDB's deadlock detector resolved by aborting one of the transactions.
resolution: Captured InnoDB deadlock information via SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS during the incident
Identified the inconsistent lock acquisition order across two code paths
Deployed a hotfix enforcing a consistent table update order across all order submission paths
Added exponential backoff to the existing retry logic to reduce retry storm amplification
Monitored deadlock counter and confirmed it returned to near zero after the fix
Verified order submission success rate returned to over 99 percent
preventive_actions: Enforce a documented standard lock acquisition order for all multi-table transactions
Add automated deadlock detection testing under concurrent load in staging
Reduce transaction scope and duration by batching only necessary row updates
Add Innodb_deadlocks metric to the production monitoring dashboard with alerting
Consider optimistic concurrency control for high-contention inventory rows
Conduct a code review audit of all multi-table transaction paths for lock ordering consistency
impact: Approximately 40 percent of order submissions failed on first attempt over a 50 minute window during peak traffic, with most succeeding on retry but contributing to elevated checkout abandonment.
lesson_learned: Deadlocks caused by inconsistent lock ordering across code paths only surface reliably under high concurrency, so lock ordering conventions must be enforced structurally rather than relying on load testing alone to catch them.

title: MongoDB Replica Set Split-Brain Condition After Network Partition Between Data Centers
description: A network partition between two data centers isolated the MongoDB replica set's primary from a majority of its secondaries, causing an election in the majority partition while the isolated primary continued briefly accepting writes before stepping down, risking divergent data.

root_cause: A fiber cut on the primary inter-data-center link caused a network partition that isolated the original primary node along with one secondary from the remaining majority in the other data center; per MongoDB's replica set protocol the original primary correctly stepped down once it detected it could not reach a majority, but a small window of writes accepted just before step-down had to be rolled back once connectivity was restored and the replica set reconciled around the new primary.
resolution: Confirmed via replica set status that a valid new primary had been elected in the majority partition
Verified the original primary correctly stepped down and did not continue accepting writes after majority loss
Once network connectivity was restored, allowed automatic rollback of the small set of divergent writes on the former primary
Extracted rolled-back documents from the rollback data files for manual review and reconciliation
Replayed reconcilable writes into the application via a manual reprocessing script
Notified the small number of affected users whose profile updates required manual reconciliation
Identified the dual-primary condition via replica set status monitoring
Waited for network connectivity to restore between availability zones
Allowed MongoDB's automatic rollback process to reconcile the divergent oplog
Reviewed rolled-back writes to assess impact on active user sessions
Forced re-authentication for the small number of affected sessions
Verified the replica set stabilized with a single primary and healthy secondaries
preventive_actions: Increase network redundancy between data centers with a secondary diverse-path link
Configure write concern majority for all critical profile writes to avoid rollback-prone acknowledgments
Add explicit alerting on replica set network partition events distinct from generic heartbeat failures
Document a rollback data reconciliation runbook for operations teams
Distribute replica set members across three data centers to reduce split-brain risk from a two-site partition
Conduct regular network partition failure drills using chaos engineering tools
Change write concern to majority for the session-store replica set
Review replica set member placement to ensure a true majority-tolerant topology
Add alerting for replica set elections and rollback events
Add cross-AZ network health monitoring with alerting on partition detection
Document a runbook for manual intervention during extended split-brain scenarios
impact: Write availability was degraded for approximately 90 seconds during the election, and a small number of writes affecting 340 user profile documents required manual reconciliation after rollback.
lesson_learned: Replica sets spanning only two data centers remain vulnerable to split-brain-adjacent rollback scenarios during partitions; distributing members across at least three sites and using majority write concern significantly reduces the risk of unacknowledged writes being lost.

Add rate limiting on invalidation requests within the deploy pipeline
Add origin-side rate limiting or circuit breaking to protect against cache-miss storms
Add monitoring for CloudFront cache hit ratio with alerting on sudden drops
Add a deploy pipeline safeguard preventing more than one deploy per short window
impact: API latency was significantly degraded for approximately 15 minutes, with a subset of requests timing out, affecting mobile and web clients relying on the API.

title: Elasticsearch Cluster Turned Red After Disk Watermark Breach on Data Nodes
description: The Elasticsearch cluster powering product search transitioned to red health status after several data nodes exceeded the flood-stage disk watermark, causing Elasticsearch to enforce a read-only index block and leaving multiple primary shards unassigned.
symptoms: Product search returning intermittent errors and empty result sets

Search queries still succeeding but returning increasingly stale results

Shard allocation showing multiple unassigned shards

2025-03-18T10:50:11Z ERROR cluster_block_exception: index [products-v12] blocked by: FORBIDDEN/12/index read-only

affected_components: Elasticsearch data nodes es-data-03 and es-data-05
root_cause: The index lifecycle management policy responsible for deleting old daily search log indices had a misconfigured role permission after a recent security update, causing the automated cleanup job to silently fail for two weeks, which allowed disk usage to grow unchecked until data nodes crossed the flood-stage watermark and triggered a cluster-wide read-only block.
resolution: Identified the three data nodes exceeding the flood-stage watermark via disk usage monitoring
Manually deleted the oldest unnecessary daily log indices to free disk space
Cleared the read-only index block cluster-wide using the cluster settings API
Fixed the ILM policy role permissions that had blocked automated cleanup
Triggered shard reallocation and confirmed cluster health returned to green
Verified product search functionality restored to normal error rates
Identified the flood-stage watermark breach via Elasticsearch cluster health API
Located and deleted several outdated, unused product index versions
Reclaimed sufficient disk space to drop nodes below the flood-stage threshold
Manually removed the read-only index block on affected indices
Triggered shard reallocation to resolve unassigned shards
Verified cluster health returned to green and indexing resumed
preventive_actions: Add disk usage alerting at the high watermark threshold well before flood stage is reached
Add automated testing for ILM policy execution success as part of the security update change process
Provision additional disk headroom or implement hot-warm-cold tiering for log indices
Add a synthetic check verifying ILM cleanup jobs actually delete expected indices daily
Document manual emergency disk space recovery procedure in the on-call runbook
Set up cross-team notification for any IAM or role permission changes affecting Elasticsearch service accounts
Fix the index lifecycle management age threshold configuration
Add disk usage alerting well below the high watermark, at 75%
Add automated weekly audit of index sizes and retention compliance
Increase data node storage capacity to provide additional headroom
Add a runbook step for safely clearing read-only blocks after space is reclaimed
impact: Product search experienced degraded to fully broken functionality for approximately 65 minutes, affecting product discovery and search-driven conversion during the incident window.
lesson_learned: Automated index lifecycle cleanup jobs need their own success monitoring independent of disk usage alerts, since a silently failing cleanup job can take weeks to manifest as a critical incident by which time recovery requires manual intervention under pressure.

title: Route53 Misconfiguration Blackholes Traffic During DNS Migration
description: During a planned migration of the primary domain's DNS records to a new hosted zone, a missing record type caused all traffic to the main application domain to fail to resolve for a portion of global users.
symptoms: DNS resolution failing intermittently depending on resolver location
NXDOMAIN responses for the apex domain from some public resolvers
Users reporting the site was completely unreachable
Some regions unaffected due to DNS caching from before the migration
Health check services reporting the domain as down
logs: 2025-03-02T05:45:00Z INFO NS records for example.com updated to new hosted zone Z1A2B3C4D5E6
2025-03-02T05:50:12Z WARN dig example.com returning NXDOMAIN from resolver 8.8.8.8
2025-03-02T05:52:00Z ERROR Missing A/ALIAS record for apex domain in new hosted zone

2025-03-02T06:00:05Z INFO Added missing ALIAS record pointing to production ALB
2025-03-02T06:04:00Z INFO DNS resolution confirmed working from all monitored regions
affected_components: Production Application Load Balancer alias target
root_cause: During the migration to the new Route53 hosted zone, the record export and import process failed to carry over the apex domain's ALIAS record pointing to the production load balancer, and the omission was not caught in the pre-cutover validation checklist because the checklist only verified NS delegation and a sample of subdomains.
resolution: Confirmed NS delegation had propagated correctly to the new hosted zone
Queried the new hosted zone directly and found the apex ALIAS record missing
Manually created the missing ALIAS record pointing to the production ALB
Verified resolution from multiple public DNS resolvers globally
Monitored uptime checks until all regions reported healthy
Communicated resolution status to stakeholders and support teams
preventive_actions: Expand the pre-cutover checklist to verify every record type, not just NS and a sample
Automate a full record comparison between old and new hosted zones before cutover
Stage DNS migrations with a lower TTL well in advance to reduce blast radius
Add synthetic DNS resolution monitoring from multiple global regions
Require a second engineer to independently verify record parity before cutover
impact: The main application domain was unreachable for a portion of global users for approximately 19 minutes, with impact varying by resolver caching state.
lesson_learned: DNS migrations require exhaustive record-level verification rather than spot-checking, since a single missing record type at the apex domain can blackhole all traffic despite correct NS delegation.

title: Consumer Lag Spike From Kafka Rebalance Storm After Rolling Deployment
description: A rolling deployment of the analytics-consumer service triggered a prolonged consumer group rebalance storm on the click-events Kafka topic because session timeout and heartbeat settings were too aggressive for the pod restart cadence, causing repeated partition reassignments and stalled processing.
symptoms: Consumer lag on click-events topic growing into the millions of messages
Frequent rebalance log entries during the rolling deployment window
Processing throughput dropping to near zero during active rebalances
Kafka broker logs showing repeated member leave and join events
Downstream analytics dashboards showing data gaps
Consumer group lag climbing continuously across multiple topics
Frequent 'Rebalance in progress' log messages from consumer instances
Consumer group generation ID incrementing rapidly
Downstream services depending on processed events experiencing delayed data
Broker logs showing repeated JoinGroup and SyncGroup requests
logs: kafka: [GroupCoordinator] Preparing to rebalance group analytics-consumer-group
kafka: [GroupCoordinator] Member analytics-consumer-7 has left the group
consumer: Commit failed since the group has already rebalanced
kafka: [GroupCoordinator] Stabilized group analytics-consumer-group generation 214
consumer-lag-exporter: click-events partition 12 lag 482103
kafka: session timeout expired, removing member from group analytics-consumer-group
2025-03-21T09:20:02Z INFO Consumer group event-processors rebalance triggered, generation 812
2025-03-21T09:20:15Z WARN Rebalance in progress, consumer instance-4 could not commit offsets
2025-03-21T09:21:00Z INFO Consumer group event-processors rebalance triggered, generation 813
2025-03-21T09:22:30Z WARN Consumer lag for topic order-events at 1.2 million messages
2025-03-21T09:23:00Z INFO Consumer group event-processors rebalance triggered, generation 814
2025-03-21T09:40:00Z INFO Rebalance stabilized at generation 815, session timeout increased
root_cause: The consumer group's session.timeout.ms was set to 10 seconds while the rolling deployment restarted pods faster than consumers could gracefully leave the group, causing the coordinator to detect false member failures and trigger a new rebalance for every pod restart, and with 40 pods rolling sequentially this produced dozens of consecutive rebalances that each paused processing for all members.
resolution: Paused the rolling deployment to stop triggering additional rebalances
Increased session.timeout.ms and max.poll.interval.ms to more tolerant values
Enabled cooperative sticky partition assignment strategy to reduce rebalance impact
Resumed the rolling deployment with the new consumer configuration
Monitored consumer lag until it drained back to near zero
Verified analytics dashboards backfilled the gapped data correctly
Identified the repeated rebalance pattern via consumer group generation ID changes
Paused the rolling restart to allow the group time to stabilize
Temporarily increased session.timeout.ms and max.poll.interval.ms for the consumer group
Resumed the rolling restart with the adjusted timeout configuration
Monitored consumer lag until it began draining consistently
Verified all consumer instances joined a single stable generation
preventive_actions: Adopt cooperative rebalancing protocol as the standard consumer configuration
Tune session and heartbeat timeouts to comfortably exceed expected pod restart duration
Use rolling deployment strategies with longer pauses between consumer pod restarts
Add consumer lag alerting with a rate-of-change trigger, not just absolute threshold
Add deployment pre-checks validating consumer group stability before proceeding to next batch
Document Kafka consumer tuning guidelines for all teams operating consumer groups
Right-size session.timeout.ms and max.poll.interval.ms based on actual processing latency
Add monitoring specifically for rebalance frequency, alerting on rapid successive rebalances
Reduce batch processing time or increase batch size limits to improve heartbeat reliability
Stagger rolling restarts with longer delays between instance replacements
Add consumer lag alerting with a threshold tuned to business SLA requirements
impact: Real-time analytics processing was degraded for approximately 45 minutes during the deployment window, with consumer lag peaking at nearly 500,000 messages before draining.
lesson_learned: Consumer group timeout settings must be tuned relative to actual deployment and restart cadences, since aggressive timeouts optimized for fast failure detection can instead cause self-inflicted rebalance storms during routine rolling deployments.

title: RabbitMQ Queue Backlog From Consumer Crash Loop on Email Delivery Service
description: The email-delivery service consumers began crash-looping after a malformed message poisoned the queue, and because the consumer lacked a dead-letter exchange configuration, the same message was repeatedly redelivered and requeued after each crash, blocking all subsequent messages in the queue from being processed.
symptoms: RabbitMQ queue depth on email-outbound growing continuously
Consumer process restarting every few seconds in container logs
Head-of-line blocking preventing any emails from being sent
Management UI showing high message redelivery count
Alerting for queue depth exceeding threshold firing repeatedly
logs: rabbitmq: queue email-outbound has 0 consumers, messages 48213
consumer: [ERROR] Uncaught exception parsing message: Unexpected token in JSON
consumer: process exited with code 1, restarting
rabbitmq: channel closed, reason: consumer acknowledgement timeout
rabbitmq: message redelivered, delivery_tag 4021, redelivered=true
systemd: email-consumer.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 214
root_cause: A malformed message was published by an upstream service due to a serialization bug during a partial deploy, and because the email-delivery consumer had no dead-letter exchange or malformed-message handling, every time the consumer attempted to parse the poison message it threw an unhandled exception, crashed, and RabbitMQ automatically requeued the unacknowledged message at the front of the queue, creating an infinite crash loop that blocked all subsequent messages behind it.
resolution: Identified the poison message using the RabbitMQ management UI get-message inspection feature
Manually acknowledged and discarded the malformed message from the queue
Verified the consumer resumed processing the remaining backlog normally
Rolled back the upstream service's partial deploy that introduced the serialization bug
Monitored queue depth until it drained to near zero
Confirmed email delivery latency returned to normal service levels
preventive_actions: Configure a dead-letter exchange for all consumer queues to isolate poison messages
Add message schema validation at the point of publish to reject malformed messages early
Wrap consumer message parsing logic in try-catch blocks with explicit error handling paths
Add alerting for consumer restart count exceeding a threshold within a time window
Add a maximum redelivery count policy to move repeatedly failing messages to a parking queue
Include poison message handling in the standard consumer service template used by all teams
impact: Email delivery was completely halted for approximately 35 minutes, delaying transactional emails including password resets and order confirmations for all users during the window.
lesson_learned: Consumers without dead-letter handling are vulnerable to complete service outage from a single malformed message, since default requeue behavior can turn one bad message into an infinite head-of-line blocking crash loop.

title: Redis Cache Stampede After Mass Key Eviction Under Memory Pressure
description: A sudden increase in product catalog size caused Redis to hit its maxmemory limit and evict a large portion of cached keys simultaneously, resulting in a stampede of requests hitting the database directly.
symptoms: Database CPU utilization jumping from 20% to 95%
API latency for product listing endpoints increasing tenfold

title: Site-Wide 502 Errors After NGINX Configuration Reload Failure
description: An automated configuration deployment attempted to reload NGINX with an updated upstream server list, but a syntax error in a newly added location block caused the reload to fail, leaving some worker processes running the old configuration while others failed to start, resulting in inconsistent routing and widespread 502 errors.
symptoms: Intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors across all site traffic
Some requests succeeding while others failed randomly
nginx -t syntax validation reporting an error after the fact
New NGINX worker processes failing to spawn
Old worker processes still handling some traffic inconsistently
logs: nginx: [emerg] unexpected "}" in /etc/nginx/conf.d/upstreams.conf:42
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test failed
systemd: nginx.service: Reload failed, keeping old configuration active for existing workers
nginx: worker process 21044 exited with code 1

root_cause: The configuration deployment pipeline applied the new upstreams.conf file and issued an nginx -s reload without first running nginx -t to validate syntax, and a missing closing brace introduced by a templating bug caused the reload to fail; because NGINX correctly refused to load the broken configuration but some servers in the fleet had already partially applied the change through a separate file distribution step, the fleet ended up in an inconsistent state across nodes.
resolution: Identified the syntax error in upstreams.conf using nginx -t on an affected host
Reverted the configuration file to the last known-good version across the entire fleet
Issued a clean nginx -s reload after confirming syntax validation passed
Verified all worker processes were running the same, corrected configuration
Monitored 502 error rate until it returned to zero across all edge nodes
Conducted a fleet-wide configuration consistency check to confirm uniformity
preventive_actions: Mandate nginx -t validation as a required, blocking step before any reload in the deployment pipeline
Add atomic configuration deployment so all nodes receive and apply changes together rather than sequentially
Add automated rollback triggered by reload failure or elevated 502 rate post-deploy
Implement canary deployment for NGINX configuration changes to a small subset of edge nodes first
Add configuration templating unit tests to catch syntax errors before deployment
Add fleet-wide configuration drift detection running continuously
impact: Approximately 30 percent of site traffic received intermittent 502 errors for 18 minutes until the configuration was fully reverted across the fleet.
lesson_learned: Configuration reloads must be gated by mandatory syntax validation and applied atomically across a fleet, since a partially applied change can leave a cluster in a worse, more inconsistent state than either the old or new configuration alone.

title: Intermittent 503 Errors From HAProxy Backend Health Check Flapping
description: HAProxy began marking backend API servers as DOWN and UP repeatedly within short intervals after a change to the health check endpoint introduced variable response times, causing HAProxy's default health check timeout to intermittently be exceeded under normal load.
symptoms: Intermittent 503 Service Unavailable responses from the API gateway
HAProxy stats page showing backend servers flapping between UP and DOWN
Uneven load distribution as some healthy backends were temporarily removed from rotation
Backend server logs showing no actual errors during marked-DOWN periods
Health check response time occasionally exceeding 2 seconds
logs: haproxy: Server api_backend/server3 is DOWN, reason: Layer7 timeout, check duration: 2003ms
haproxy: Server api_backend/server3 is UP, reason: Layer7 check passed
haproxy: Backend api_backend has no server available!
backend-app: GET /health 200 in 1850ms
haproxy: 503 SERVICE UNAVAILABLE returned to client, no server available
haproxy: Health check timeout is set to 2000ms
root_cause: A recent change added a downstream dependency check to the /health endpoint that queried a slow-responding internal metadata service, occasionally pushing health check response times above HAProxy's configured 2000ms timeout, which caused HAProxy to mark otherwise healthy backends as DOWN whenever the dependency check happened to be slow, and with multiple backends flapping simultaneously the pool occasionally had zero available servers.
resolution: Correlated HAProxy DOWN events with backend health check response time logs
Identified the newly added slow dependency check in the health endpoint as the cause
Reverted the health endpoint to a lightweight check that did not depend on the slow metadata service
Increased HAProxy health check timeout as an additional safety margin
Verified backend servers stabilized in the UP state consistently
Monitored 503 error rate returning to zero
preventive_actions: Keep health check endpoints lightweight and free of slow downstream dependency calls
Separate liveness checks from deeper readiness or dependency checks using distinct endpoints
Increase HAProxy health check timeout and add fall/rise thresholds to reduce sensitivity to transient slowness
Add monitoring for health check response time distribution, not just pass or fail status
Require load testing of any health endpoint change before production deployment
Document health check design guidelines distinguishing liveness from readiness semantics
impact: Approximately 8 percent of API requests received intermittent 503 errors over a 2 hour period as backend capacity fluctuated due to flapping health checks.
lesson_learned: Health check endpoints should never depend on slow or unreliable downstream services, since doing so couples overall service availability, as perceived by the load balancer, to the latency characteristics of unrelated dependencies.
