title: PostgreSQL Table Bloat From Long-Running Transaction Blocks Vacuum
description: A reporting query left open in an idle transaction for over 10 hours prevented autovacuum from reclaiming dead tuples on the orders table, leading to significant table bloat and degrading query performance.
symptoms: Query latency on the orders table gradually increasing over several hours
Table size growing disproportionately to actual row count
autovacuum logs showing repeated skipped runs on the orders table
pg_stat_activity showing a transaction idle in transaction for hours
Increased sequential scan time reported in slow query logs
logs: 2025-03-08T16:20:00Z INFO Reporting job connected, transaction started
2025-03-08T16:22:00Z INFO Reporting job query completed, connection left open
2025-03-08T18:00:00Z WARN autovacuum: skipping vacuum of orders, table locked by pid 20441
2025-03-09T00:00:00Z WARN orders table bloat estimated at 3.2x normal size
2025-03-09T02:30:00Z WARN Query planner choosing sequential scan due to bloated index statistics
2025-03-09T02:45:12Z INFO Idle transaction pid 20441 terminated by DBA
root_cause: The reporting service's connection pool did not enforce a maximum idle-in-transaction timeout, so a reporting job that completed its query but never explicitly committed or closed its transaction held a snapshot open for over 10 hours, which prevented autovacuum from cleaning up dead tuples generated by normal order table churn, causing significant bloat.
resolution: Queried pg_stat_activity to identify long-running idle transactions
Identified the reporting service connection as the culprit via application name
Terminated the idle transaction to unblock autovacuum
Manually triggered a VACUUM ANALYZE on the orders table
Monitored query latency and table size until they returned to normal
Notified the reporting service team about the connection handling issue
preventive_actions: Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout at the database level
Update the reporting service to explicitly commit or rollback after each query
Add monitoring and alerting for transactions idle for over 10 minutes
Add periodic reporting of table bloat estimates to the DBA dashboard
Review all long-running batch and reporting jobs for similar connection patterns
impact: Query latency on order-related endpoints gradually degraded over roughly 10 hours, with the most significant impact in the final 2 hours before resolution.
resolution_time: 25 minutes (from detection to resolution; underlying issue present for 10 hours)
lesson_learned: Idle-in-transaction connections silently block vacuum and cause slow-building performance degradation that is easy to miss until it becomes severe; database-level idle transaction timeouts are a cheap and effective safeguard.

title: Service Mesh Traffic Failures Due to Istio Sidecar Injection Failure After Webhook Misconfiguration
description: New pods across several namespaces began starting without the Istio Envoy sidecar container after the istio-sidecar-injector mutating webhook began failing its own TLS certificate validation, silently skipping injection and leaving new pods unable to communicate within the mesh.
symptoms: New pods running with only 1 of 2 expected containers
mTLS connection failures between services expecting sidecar-to-sidecar communication
Pods lacking sidecars able to reach plaintext endpoints but failing against mTLS-enforced services
kube-apiserver logs showing webhook call failures
istiod logs showing certificate expiration warnings
logs: kube-apiserver: failed calling webhook sidecar-injector.istio.io: x509: certificate has expired
istiod: Generated new CA certificate, webhook cert rotation required
kube-apiserver: admission webhook denied the request but failurePolicy=Ignore, proceeding without mutation
app: [ERROR] upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers, reset reason: connection failure
istio-proxy: TLS handshake error: certificate verify failed
kube-apiserver: webhook sidecar-injector.istio.io not accessible, timeout
affected_components: Newly created pods across mesh namespaces
root_cause: The istiod-managed webhook TLS certificate expired because a certificate rotation automation job had failed silently for several weeks due to an unrelated RBAC permission change, and because the mutating webhook was configured with failurePolicy set to Ignore, pods continued to be created without sidecar injection instead of blocking deployment, masking the underlying certificate problem until mTLS-dependent traffic began failing.
resolution: Identified expired webhook certificate as the root cause via kube-apiserver audit logs
Manually triggered istiod certificate regeneration for the webhook
Updated the MutatingWebhookConfiguration with the new CA bundle
Restarted or rolled affected deployments to trigger correct sidecar injection on pod recreation
Verified mTLS connectivity restored between mesh services
Fixed the underlying RBAC permission issue blocking the certificate rotation automation
preventive_actions: Add alerting for webhook certificate expiration well in advance, separate from generic cert monitoring
Change failurePolicy to Fail for the sidecar injector webhook in critical namespaces to prevent silent skips
Add automated testing that verifies certificate rotation automation actually succeeds, not just that it ran
Add a synthetic check confirming new pods always receive the expected container count
Audit RBAC changes for any impact on istiod's certificate management service account
Document istio control plane certificate lifecycle and manual recovery steps in the mesh runbook
impact: New pod deployments across 5 namespaces over a 3 hour window lacked sidecar injection, causing mTLS communication failures for approximately 12 services until affected pods were recreated with the fix in place.
lesson_learned: Mutating webhooks configured with a permissive failurePolicy can silently degrade a critical platform capability like service mesh sidecar injection without any obvious failure signal, so security-relevant webhooks should generally fail closed with strong monitoring around their own health.

title: Total Loss of Metrics Ingestion After Prometheus Local Storage Disk Filled
description: The primary Prometheus server stopped ingesting new metrics entirely after its local TSDB storage volume filled to 100 percent capacity, caused by an unexpected explosion in time series cardinality from a newly instrumented service that used unbounded label values.
symptoms: Grafana dashboards showing no new data points for the past several hours
Prometheus target scrape status showing errors across all jobs
Alertmanager showing stale or missing alerts
Prometheus process logs showing write errors to the WAL
Disk usage on the Prometheus data volume at 100 percent
logs: prometheus: level=error msg="CorruptionErr: write /data/wal/00001823: no space left on device"
prometheus: level=warn msg="Error opening memory series storage" err="no space left on device"
node-exporter: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/data"} 0
prometheus: level=error msg="target scrape failed" reason="context deadline exceeded"
prometheus: level=info msg="Head GC completed" duration=45.2s
prometheus: level=error msg="compaction failed" err="no space left on device"
root_cause: A newly deployed microservice exposed a Prometheus metrics endpoint that included a raw user ID as a label value on a request counter metric, and because user ID is effectively unbounded cardinality, the number of unique time series grew into the millions within days, rapidly consuming disk space allocated for Prometheus's local TSDB well beyond what capacity planning had assumed for stable, low-cardinality metrics.
resolution: Identified the offending metric and its high-cardinality label using Prometheus TSDB status and cardinality analysis tools
Blocked scraping of the offending metric by updating the scrape config with metric_relabel_configs to drop it
Manually deleted old and unnecessary blocks from the TSDB data directory to free emergency disk space
Restarted Prometheus and confirmed successful WAL replay and scraping resumed
Verified Grafana dashboards and Alertmanager began receiving fresh data
Worked with the offending service team to remove the unbounded label from their instrumentation
preventive_actions: Add cardinality limits and alerting on total active time series count in Prometheus
Require metrics instrumentation review for new services to check for unbounded label values
Provision additional disk headroom with automated alerting well before 100 percent utilization
Migrate to a remote-write long-term storage backend to reduce reliance on local disk capacity
Add a linting check in CI that flags common high-cardinality label patterns like user IDs or request IDs
Document metrics instrumentation best practices covering label cardinality guidance for all engineering teams
impact: All metrics-based monitoring and alerting was unavailable for approximately 3 hours, significantly reducing visibility into the health of the production environment during that window.
lesson_learned: Unbounded label cardinality from a single misconfigured metric can silently exhaust monitoring infrastructure capacity and take down observability for the entire platform, so cardinality guardrails need to be enforced both technically and through instrumentation review process.

title: Cluster Left in Broken State After Failed Helm Release Rollback During ArgoCD Sync
description: An ArgoCD automated sync attempted to roll back the payments-api Helm release after detecting a failed health check on a new version, but the rollback itself failed midway due to a CRD version mismatch, leaving the release in a pending-rollback state with some resources on the new version and others on the old.
symptoms: ArgoCD application showing OutOfSync and Degraded status simultaneously
Helm release status stuck in pending-rollback
Some payments-api pods running the new image while others ran the old image
kubectl get pods showing inconsistent ReplicaSet ownership
ArgoCD sync operations failing with a generic Helm error
logs: argocd: Sync operation failed: Helm rollback failed: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress
helm: Error: UPGRADE FAILED: release payments-api failed, and has been rolled back due to atomic being set
helm: Error: rollback failed: PaymentPolicy.policy.example.com is invalid: apiVersion policy.example.com/v1 not found
argocd-application-controller: comparison error caused by helm rollback in progress
kubectl: replicaset payments-api-7f9d created but not scaled by controller
argocd: application payments-api health check Degraded reason: rollback incomplete
root_cause: The new chart version introduced a custom resource using an updated CRD apiVersion that had not yet been applied to the cluster, so when the automated rollback attempted to revert PaymentPolicy resources back to the old apiVersion format, Kubernetes rejected the operation as invalid since the old apiVersion had already been removed from the CRD's served versions, leaving Helm's release history in an inconsistent pending-rollback state.
resolution: Manually inspected the Helm release history using helm history payments-api to understand the stuck state
Applied the missing CRD version definition to support both old and new apiVersions temporarily
Manually completed the rollback using helm rollback with the --force flag after CRD compatibility was restored
Verified all payments-api pods converged to a single consistent version
Resumed ArgoCD automated sync and confirmed Synced and Healthy status
Reviewed the chart's CRD versioning strategy with the owning team
preventive_actions: Require CRD apiVersion compatibility checks as part of chart pre-upgrade hooks
Maintain CRDs as a separately versioned, backward-compatible deployment step from application charts
Disable ArgoCD automated self-heal for releases involving CRD changes, requiring manual approval instead
Add a Helm chart linting step in CI that flags removal of previously served CRD apiVersions
Add ArgoCD sync wave ordering to apply CRDs before dependent custom resources
Document manual Helm release recovery procedures for pending-rollback states in the GitOps runbook
impact: The payments-api service ran a split-version deployment for approximately 40 minutes, with some inconsistent behavior in policy evaluation logic until the cluster converged to a single version.
lesson_learned: Automated rollback mechanisms assume the previous state is always reachable, but CRD apiVersion changes can make rollback itself impossible, so CRD lifecycle changes need to be decoupled from application releases and treated with additional caution around backward compatibility.

title: Secrets Access Outage After Vault Cluster Auto-Sealed Following Storage Backend Failure
description: The HashiCorp Vault cluster automatically sealed itself after losing connectivity to its Consul storage backend during a network maintenance event, blocking all applications from retrieving dynamic database credentials and other secrets until the cluster was manually unsealed.
symptoms: Applications failing to start with permission denied errors retrieving secrets
Vault status command showing sealed true across all cluster nodes
Vault API returning 503 with error Vault is sealed
Consul cluster showing leader election activity during the same window
Dynamic database credential renewal failures across dependent services
logs: vault: [ERROR] core: failed to acquire lock, storage backend unavailable
vault: [WARN] core: vault is sealed
consul: [ERROR] agent: failed to sync remote state: rpc error: leader unknown
vault: [INFO] core: seal configuration missing, cannot unseal
app: [ERROR] failed to renew database lease: permission denied, vault sealed
vault: [ERROR] http: request failed error=Vault is sealed
consul: [INFO] raft: node ... entering leader state
affected_components: All applications retrieving secrets at runtime
root_cause: A network maintenance change unexpectedly disrupted connectivity between two of three Consul server nodes, triggering a Consul leader election, and during the brief period without a stable Consul leader, Vault lost its ability to communicate with its storage backend, causing all Vault nodes to automatically seal as a safety mechanism designed to prevent operating without reliable storage consistency.
resolution: Confirmed Consul cluster had re-established a stable leader after the network maintenance completed
Gathered the required quorum of unseal key holders per the organization's key-sharding policy
Manually ran vault operator unseal with each key share on all sealed Vault nodes
Verified Vault returned to unsealed and active status via vault status
Confirmed applications successfully resumed retrieving and renewing secrets
Reviewed the network maintenance change process with the networking team to prevent recurrence
preventive_actions: Coordinate network maintenance windows explicitly with teams operating quorum-based systems like Consul and Vault
Implement Vault auto-unseal using a cloud KMS to eliminate dependency on manual key-holder availability during incidents
Increase Consul server node count and improve network path redundancy between Consul nodes
Add alerting specifically for Vault seal status changes, distinct from general health checks
Add alerting for Consul leader election events indicating potential underlying network instability
Document and rehearse the manual unseal procedure regularly with all designated key holders
impact: All secret retrieval and dynamic credential renewal across the platform was unavailable for approximately 25 minutes, causing several dependent services to fail startup or lose database connectivity as credentials expired.
lesson_learned: Vault's automatic sealing behavior, while a critical safety feature, means that its availability is only as strong as its storage backend's availability; migrating to auto-unseal removes the operational fragility of depending on manually available key holders during an incident.

title: Public API Outage Due to Unnoticed SSL Certificate Expiry on Ingress Controller
description: The public-facing API gateway became completely unreachable over HTTPS at midnight when the TLS certificate served by the NGINX ingress controller expired, because the cert-manager renewal job had been failing silently for weeks due to an unresolved DNS-01 challenge issue with a recently migrated DNS provider.
symptoms: All HTTPS requests to api.example.com failing with certificate expired errors in clients
Browser and curl clients showing NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID or equivalent
cert-manager Certificate resource showing Ready False for an extended period
Ingress controller logs showing TLS handshake failures
Monitoring showing synthetic HTTPS health checks failing exactly at midnight
logs: cert-manager: Certificate api-example-com-tls not ready: DNS record propagation check failed
cert-manager: challenge validation failed: NXDOMAIN looking up _acme-challenge.api.example.com
nginx-ingress: SSL_do_handshake() failed, certificate has expired
client: curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired
cert-manager: Renewal of certificate api-example-com-tls scheduled for 2025-03-01 failed 14 times
kube-events: Warning FailedChallenge cert-manager unable to solve challenge for domain api.example.com
root_cause: A DNS provider migration completed three weeks prior updated the primary DNS records but did not update the API credentials cert-manager used for the DNS-01 challenge with the new provider, causing every renewal attempt to fail the ACME challenge validation silently in the background while the existing valid certificate masked the problem until its natural expiration date arrived.
resolution: Identified the repeated failed challenge validation events in cert-manager logs and Kubernetes events
Updated the cert-manager DNS provider API credentials to match the new DNS provider
Manually triggered a new certificate issuance request
Verified the ACME DNS-01 challenge completed successfully with the corrected credentials
Confirmed the new certificate was picked up by the ingress controller and HTTPS access restored
Notified customers of the outage and root cause via status page update
preventive_actions: Add alerting for cert-manager Certificate resources in a non-Ready state for more than 24 hours
Add alerting for certificate expiration approaching within 14 days as a separate safety net independent of cert-manager
Include DNS provider credential validation as an explicit step in any DNS migration runbook
Add synthetic monitoring that checks actual certificate expiry dates on all public endpoints daily
Implement dual ACME challenge methods, such as both DNS-01 and HTTP-01, for redundancy
Conduct a quarterly audit of all cert-manager Certificate resources for renewal health
impact: The public API was completely unreachable over HTTPS for approximately 50 minutes starting at midnight, affecting all customer integrations and mobile app functionality dependent on the API.
lesson_learned: Certificate renewal automation failures are dangerously silent because the existing valid certificate continues to work right up until the hard expiration deadline, so renewal health needs independent, expiry-date-based alerting rather than relying solely on the renewal job's own reported status.

title: Silent Data Pipeline Gap From Failed Nightly Cron Job After Timezone Change
description: The nightly data aggregation Kubernetes CronJob silently stopped producing output for three consecutive days after a base image update changed the container's default timezone, causing the job's internal date-range calculation logic to compute an incorrect processing window that resulted in querying an already-processed date range and writing zero new rows without raising any error.
symptoms: Downstream analytics reports missing three days of aggregated data
CronJob pod completing successfully with exit code 0 every night
No error logs or alerts triggered since the job technically succeeded
Data warehouse table row count flat for the affected date range
Business stakeholders noticing anomalies in weekly trend reports before engineering was alerted
logs: cronjob: Job data-aggregation-28459123 completed successfully
app: [INFO] Processing date range 2025-03-16 to 2025-03-16
app: [INFO] Query returned 0 rows for date range, writing empty batch
app: [INFO] Aggregation job finished, rows_written=0, duration=12s
kube-events: Normal SawCompletedJob CronJob data-aggregation successfully completed
app: [INFO] Container timezone: UTC (previously America/New_York)
root_cause: A routine base image update changed the container's default timezone from America/New_York to UTC, and the job's date-range calculation used the local system time to determine yesterday's date for processing, so with the timezone shift the calculated date range shifted by several hours in a way that caused it to compute a date that had already been fully processed the previous night, resulting in a query against already-aggregated data that correctly returned zero new rows and exited successfully.
resolution: Investigated the data gap after being alerted by business stakeholders reviewing weekly reports
Reviewed job logs and identified the processed date range was incorrect for three consecutive runs
Traced the incorrect date calculation to the timezone change in the updated base image
Fixed the date-range calculation to explicitly use UTC regardless of container timezone configuration
Manually re-ran the aggregation job with corrected date ranges for the three missed days
Verified the data warehouse backfilled correctly and downstream reports reflected accurate data
preventive_actions: Refactor all date and time calculations in scheduled jobs to explicitly specify UTC rather than relying on system default timezone
Add data quality validation checks that alert when a job writes zero rows unexpectedly for a non-empty expected date range
Add row count anomaly detection comparing each run's output against historical baselines
Require explicit timezone environment variable pinning in all CronJob container specifications
Add integration tests that verify date-range calculation logic across timezone changes
Include base image timezone configuration as a reviewed item in the base image update change process
impact: Three days of aggregated business analytics data were missing from downstream reports, affecting weekly trend analysis and causing minor decision-making delays until the gap was identified and backfilled.
lesson_learned: Jobs that exit successfully with zero output are far more dangerous than jobs that fail loudly, since success-based monitoring alone cannot catch silent logic errors; data pipelines need explicit row-count and data-quality validation independent of job exit status.

symptoms: RabbitMQ management UI showing queue depth for transactional-email growing steadily

impact: Transactional emails including password resets and order receipts were delayed for approximately 20 minutes for roughly 8,400 queued messages.
lesson_learned: Dependency upgrades, even minor ones, can silently break assumptions in application code; CI coverage of critical startup paths and fast-failing readiness checks would have caught this before it reached production.

title: HAProxy Serving Traffic to Stale Backend Due to Delayed Health Check Detection
description: A subset of user requests received connection errors after one backend server became unresponsive but HAProxy continued routing traffic to it for several minutes before marking it down.
symptoms: Sporadic connection refused and timeout errors for a fraction of requests
HAProxy stats page showing one backend still marked UP despite being unresponsive

resolution: Identified app-backend-3 as unresponsive via server process investigation
Manually removed app-backend-3 from the HAProxy backend pool
Restarted the hung application process on app-backend-3
Re-added app-backend-3 to the pool after confirming it passed health checks
Reduced health check interval to 5 seconds and fall count to 2 for faster detection
Verified no further connection errors occurred after the configuration change
preventive_actions: Standardize faster health check intervals across all HAProxy backend pools
Add application-level health checks that verify thread pool responsiveness, not just port reachability
Add HAProxy stats monitoring with alerting on backend state transitions
Add automatic retry logic on the client side for transient connection errors
Investigate and address the root cause of the hung thread pool on app-backend-3
impact: Approximately 2% of requests over a 15-minute window received connection errors before the unresponsive backend was manually removed from rotation.
lesson_learned: Health check intervals and fall thresholds directly determine how long a load balancer continues sending traffic to a failed backend; these should be tuned aggressively for services where even brief exposure to a bad backend is costly.

title: Istio mTLS Failures Across Mesh After Certificate Rotation Misconfiguration
description: Following an automated certificate rotation event, service-to-service calls across the mesh began failing with TLS handshake errors as sidecar proxies held mismatched certificate trust chains.
symptoms: Widespread 503 UF errors across multiple services in the mesh
Envoy sidecar logs showing TLS handshake failures between services

2025-04-02T05:05:00Z ERROR 503 UF, upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers

root_cause: The certificate rotation process pushed the new root CA to sidecar proxies without ensuring an overlap period where both old and new root certificates were trusted simultaneously, so proxies that received the new certificate before their communication partners had rotated could not validate the still-old certificates presented by those partners, and vice versa.
resolution: Identified the TLS handshake failures as correlated with the certificate rotation event
Confirmed proxies were in inconsistent certificate generations via proxy-status
Manually triggered proxy configuration sync across all affected sidecars
Monitored proxy-status until all proxies converged on the new certificate generation
Verified mTLS connections succeeded across previously failing service pairs
Reviewed the certificate rotation process for the missing overlap window
preventive_actions: Configure certificate rotation with a dual-trust overlap period for old and new root CAs
Add automated validation that all proxies converge before considering rotation complete
Add alerting on proxy-status showing STALE configuration for longer than a few minutes
Add alerting specifically for spikes in mTLS handshake failure rates
Test certificate rotation procedures in staging before scheduling in production
impact: Inter-service communication was degraded across the mesh for approximately 15 minutes, causing elevated error rates for multiple dependent services during peak morning traffic.
lesson_learned: Certificate rotation in a mesh environment requires a deliberate dual-trust overlap window to avoid a race condition where proxies mutually distrust each other during the transition; rotation completeness should be actively verified, not assumed.

title: Prometheus Server OOM From High-Cardinality Metric Explosion
description: The central Prometheus server became unresponsive and eventually crashed after a new application deployment began emitting metrics with unbounded label cardinality, exhausting available memory.
symptoms: Prometheus web UI and API becoming slow and eventually unresponsive
Prometheus process memory usage climbing continuously without leveling off
Grafana dashboards timing out when querying affected metrics
Prometheus process eventually OOM killed by the kernel
Alertmanager reporting a gap in alert evaluation during the outage

2025-04-05T18:10:00Z WARN Head series count: 8.2 million, up from typical 1.1 million
2025-04-05T18:15:30Z ERROR Query timeout evaluating rule cpu_usage_by_request_id
2025-04-05T18:20:00Z WARN Prometheus memory usage at 98%
2025-04-05T18:22:11Z ERROR oom-killer invoked, killed process prometheus (pid 4021)
2025-04-05T18:30:00Z INFO Prometheus restarted with metric relabeling rule applied
root_cause: A new deployment of recommendation-service included a metric that used a unique per-request identifier as a label value, creating a new, permanent time series for every single request and causing the total number of active time series in Prometheus to grow by millions within hours, far exceeding available memory.
resolution: Identified the abnormal head series count growth via Prometheus internal metrics
Traced the growth to the newly deployed recommendation-service metric
Added a metric_relabel_config rule to drop the offending high-cardinality label
Restarted Prometheus to clear the excessive in-memory series after configuration fix
Verified memory usage and head series count returned to normal levels
Notified the recommendation-service team about the metric design issue
preventive_actions: Add a cardinality review step to the metrics instrumentation guidelines
Add automated alerting on head series count growth rate
Implement a cardinality limit safeguard at the Prometheus scrape config level
Add a pre-deploy check that flags new metrics with high-cardinality label candidates
Document known high-risk label patterns such as request IDs, user IDs, and timestamps
impact: Metrics collection and alerting were degraded or unavailable for approximately 30 minutes, during which several unrelated alerts may have been delayed or missed.
lesson_learned: Unbounded label cardinality is one of the most common causes of Prometheus instability; instrumentation guidelines and automated safeguards are necessary to prevent a single bad metric from taking down observability for the entire platform.

title: ArgoCD Sync Failures After CRD Version Mismatch Causes Config Drift
description: Several applications managed by ArgoCD showed persistent OutOfSync status after a cluster upgrade changed the installed version of a custom resource definition, preventing GitOps reconciliation from completing.
symptoms: ArgoCD UI showing multiple applications stuck in OutOfSync status

Compared the installed CRD schema against the manifest repository's apiVersion
Updated the affected manifests to use the current cert-manager.io/v1 apiVersion and field names

preventive_actions: Add a pre-upgrade compatibility check between cluster CRD versions and GitOps manifests
Add CI validation that manifests apply successfully against the target cluster's CRD schemas
Coordinate cluster upgrade timing with a review of dependent manifest repositories
Add ArgoCD notifications for applications remaining OutOfSync beyond a defined duration
Document the CRD upgrade process including manifest migration steps
impact: GitOps-managed configuration changes for cert-manager-related applications could not be reconciled for approximately 20 minutes, though existing running resources were unaffected.
lesson_learned: Cluster upgrades that bump operator or CRD versions must be coordinated with the GitOps manifest repositories that reference those resources, since schema changes can silently block reconciliation even when no application-level issue exists.

title: Vault Auto-Unseal Failure Blocks Application Secret Retrieval Fleet-Wide
description: Following a scheduled cloud provider maintenance event that restarted the Vault cluster's underlying nodes, Vault came back up in a sealed state and failed to auto-unseal, blocking every application from retrieving secrets on startup.

resolution: Confirmed all Vault nodes were sealed via vault status on each node

Confirmed Vault nodes successfully auto-unsealed once connectivity returned
Manually restarted stuck application pods to trigger successful secret retrieval

Maintain a documented and tested manual unseal procedure with securely stored key shares
Add alerting specifically for Vault sealed state across the cluster

Include Vault auto-unseal dependency checks in cloud maintenance impact assessments
impact: Applications requiring secret retrieval on startup were unable to launch or restart for approximately 12 minutes fleet-wide, though already-running applications with cached secrets were unaffected.
lesson_learned: Auto-unseal mechanisms create a hard dependency on external KMS connectivity that must be as resilient as Vault itself; a documented manual unseal fallback is essential for scenarios where that dependency is unavailable.

title: Nightly Backup Job Silently Failing for Weeks Due to Cron Schedule Drift
description: During a disaster recovery drill, engineers discovered that the nightly database backup job had not produced a successful backup in over three weeks, with failures going unnoticed because the failure notification webhook was also broken.
symptoms: Backup storage bucket showing no new backup files for over three weeks
Cron job execution logs present but backup completion logs absent
Slack webhook channel for backup notifications receiving no messages, success or failure
DR drill restore attempt failing due to lack of a recent recoverable backup
Backup job process exiting silently without a clear success or failure signal
logs: 2025-03-27T02:00:01Z INFO backup-job started for orders-db
2025-03-27T02:00:45Z ERROR pg_dump: connection to database failed: too many connections
2025-03-27T02:00:45Z INFO backup-job process exiting with code 0
2025-04-17T08:30:00Z WARN DR drill: no backup files found newer than 2025-03-26
2025-04-17T08:45:00Z ERROR webhook notification test failed: DNS resolution error for hooks.slack.com
2025-04-17T09:00:00Z INFO backup-job script patched to exit non-zero on pg_dump failure
root_cause: A bug in the backup script caused it to exit with status code 0 even when the underlying pg_dump command failed, so the job scheduler never recognized the backups as failing, and independently the Slack webhook used for notifications had stopped working weeks earlier due to a DNS resolution issue in the notification sidecar, meaning even a correctly-signaled failure would not have alerted anyone.
resolution: Investigated backup storage and found no successful backups in over three weeks
Reviewed backup job logs and identified the pg_dump failure being swallowed
Separately diagnosed and fixed the DNS resolution issue breaking the Slack webhook
Patched the backup script to exit non-zero and alert on any underlying command failure
Manually triggered a fresh backup and verified it completed and was restorable
Escalated to database team to resolve the connection limit issue causing pg_dump failures
preventive_actions: Add automated verification that checks for a fresh, restorable backup daily, independent of the job's own success signal
Fix exit code handling in all backup and maintenance scripts to propagate real failures
Add redundant notification channels for critical job failures, not just a single webhook
Schedule regular DR drills at a defined cadence rather than ad hoc
Add monitoring for the age of the most recent successful backup with alerting if it exceeds 24 hours
impact: The organization was without a valid disaster recovery backup for orders-db for over three weeks, representing significant unrecognized data loss risk during that window, though no actual data loss occurred.
resolution_time: 1 hour 30 minutes (discovery to fresh verified backup)
lesson_learned: A job succeeding at the process level does not mean it succeeded at its actual purpose; backup systems need independent, outcome-based verification and redundant alerting, since a single broken notification path can mask weeks of silent failure.

title: Kubernetes Node Memory Pressure Evicting Critical Pods
description: Multiple pods on worker node ip-10-0-4-21 were evicted after the kubelet detected sustained MemoryPressure, causing intermittent checkout failures during a flash-sale traffic spike.
symptoms: Pods in Evicted state on node ip-10-0-4-21
Checkout API latency p99 rising to 4s before evictions
New pods pending with FailedScheduling on same node
logs: 09:08:02 kubelet Node condition MemoryPressure is now True
09:08:04 kubelet Attempting to evict pod checkout-service-6d9f-x2p8
09:08:05 kube-scheduler Pod checkout-service-6d9f-x2p8 evicted, memory node condition
09:08:12 kubelet Attempting to evict pod recommendation-worker-3f
09:09:40 kube-controller-manager ReplicaSet checkout-service scaling up to replace evicted pods
09:10:02 kubelet Node condition MemoryPressure is now False
root_cause: Pods on the node had no memory limits set, so during the traffic spike several pods' usage grew unbounded and consumed all allocatable memory on the node, triggering kubelet's eviction manager to reclaim resources by killing pods regardless of their own health.
resolution: Identified the unbounded pods via kubectl top pod --sort-by=memory
Set explicit memory requests/limits on checkout-service and recommendation-worker Deployments
Cordoned and drained the affected node to force rescheduling onto healthier nodes
Manually triggered rollout restart of evicted Deployments
Verified pod distribution and memory headroom post-restart
preventive_actions: Enforce a LimitRange and ResourceQuota per namespace requiring memory limits
Add Prometheus alert for node MemoryPressure condition
Enable Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode to right-size requests
Load test flash-sale traffic patterns in staging before major sales events
impact: Approximately 8% of checkout requests failed or timed out over a 6-minute window during peak flash-sale traffic.
lesson_learned: Pods without memory limits are a shared-node liability — one noisy workload can evict unrelated healthy pods.

title: Docker Image Corrupted Layer Causing Container Crash Loop
description: notification-service containers entered CrashLoopBackOff immediately after a routine image pull from the internal registry, with containers exiting before application startup logs appeared.
symptoms: Container exits with code 125 before app logs print
docker pull succeeds but docker run fails instantly
Registry storage node reported intermittent disk I/O errors overnight
Only pods scheduled after 02:00 UTC affected
Image digest mismatch between manifest and local blob
logs: 14:22:01 dockerd Pulling image registry.internal/notification-service:1.42.0
14:22:07 dockerd Digest verification failed for layer sha256:9af3...
14:22:07 dockerd Error response from daemon: failed to register layer: layer not found
14:22:08 kubelet Back-off restarting failed container
14:25:00 registry-storage disk I/O error on volume /data (read-only remount)
root_cause: The registry's underlying EBS volume experienced a hardware-level I/O error during the image push, silently corrupting one layer's blob on disk while the manifest still referenced the original (correct) digest, so subsequent pulls fetched a corrupted layer that failed digest verification.
resolution: Identified the failing layer digest from dockerd error logs
Confirmed registry storage volume had entered read-only mode via cloud provider console
Failed over registry storage to the standby EBS volume
Re-pushed the affected image tag from the CI build cache to regenerate a clean layer
Force-deleted and rescheduled all crash-looping pods to re-pull the corrected image
preventive_actions: Enable registry storage checksumming/scrubbing on a nightly schedule
Add CI step to verify pushed image digest against a pull-back-and-verify check
Configure registry storage with multi-AZ replication instead of single EBS volume
Alert on registry storage volume I/O error metrics
impact: notification-service was unavailable for new deployments for 40 minutes; existing running pods were unaffected.
lesson_learned: Registry storage needs the same durability guarantees as application data — a corrupted layer fails silently until pull time.

title: Jenkins Agents Disconnected After SSH Host Key Rotation
description: All Jenkins build agents lost connectivity to the controller simultaneously after a scheduled security rotation of SSH host keys on the agent fleet, blocking every queued and scheduled build.
symptoms: All agents show 'offline' in Jenkins node dashboard
Jenkins controller logs SSH host key verification failures

07:00:20 jenkins-controller Agent build-agent-03 marked offline
07:00:20 jenkins-controller Agent build-agent-04 marked offline

resolution: Confirmed the host key rotation was legitimate via the security team's change ticket
Pulled the new host keys directly from each agent's instance metadata
Updated the Jenkins controller's known_hosts file with the new fingerprints
Restarted the Jenkins SSH agent launcher service
Verified all 12 agents reconnected and drained the backed-up build queue
preventive_actions: Add known_hosts update as a required step in the SSH key rotation runbook
Automate known_hosts sync via configuration management alongside key rotation
Add a Jenkins health check alert for agent offline count exceeding a threshold
Document a dependency link between the key-rotation and CI-infrastructure change processes
impact: All CI/CD builds were blocked for 35 minutes; 60+ builds queued and deployed late.
lesson_learned: Security rotations that touch shared trust material (host keys, certs) need cross-team coordination with every consumer of that trust store.

title: GitHub Actions Workflow Leaked Secret in Plaintext Logs
description: A GitHub Actions workflow printed a database connection string containing credentials to the public build log after a developer added a debug echo statement, exposing the secret to anyone with read access to the repository's Actions logs.
symptoms: Debug echo step outputs full DATABASE_URL including password
GitHub secret masking did not redact the value
Security scanning bot flagged the exposed log within 20 minutes
Log was publicly viewable on a public repository
logs: 11:40:02 workflow Step 'Debug env' started
11:40:02 workflow echo "Connecting with $DATABASE_URL"
11:40:03 workflow ::warning:: Value not registered as a secret, masking skipped
11:41:10 secret-scanner-bot Potential credential exposure detected in run #4821
11:42:00 security-oncall Paged: possible credential leak in public repo
root_cause: DATABASE_URL was constructed by concatenating a secret with other non-secret values inside the workflow script; GitHub's automatic log masking only redacts values that exactly match a registered secret string, so the concatenated composite string was not recognized and printed unmasked when a developer added a temporary debug echo.
resolution: Immediately rotated the exposed database credentials
Deleted the affected workflow run logs via GitHub API
Audited all recent workflow runs for the same debug pattern
Revoked and reissued all database connections using the old credential
Removed the debug echo statement from the workflow
preventive_actions: Ban raw echo of any environment variable containing 'SECRET', 'PASSWORD', or 'URL' via a pre-commit/CI lint rule
Register composite secret strings explicitly with add-mask in workflow scripts
Restrict debug/verbose workflow modes to private repositories only
Add mandatory secret-scanning gate before merging workflow file changes
impact: Production database credentials were publicly exposed for approximately 20 minutes before detection; credentials rotated as precaution, no confirmed unauthorized access.
lesson_learned: Secret masking only catches exact string matches — composite or transformed secrets need to be explicitly masked.

title: GitLab CI Pipelines Stuck Pending Due to Runner Tag Mismatch
description: After a runner fleet migration, dozens of GitLab CI pipelines remained in 'pending' status indefinitely because jobs requested a runner tag that no longer existed on any registered runner.
symptoms: Pipelines stuck in pending with 'This job is stuck, because you don't have any active runners'
No error in job logs since jobs never start
Runner fleet dashboard shows all runners online and idle
Only jobs from the newly migrated project group affected

16:06:30 gitlab-ci Job build:docker still pending (90s elapsed)
16:10:00 gitlab-ci Job build:docker still pending (390s elapsed)
root_cause: A runner fleet migration replaced the old arm64-legacy tagged runners with new runners tagged arm64, but the .gitlab-ci.yml files across multiple projects still referenced the deprecated arm64-legacy tag, and no runner advertised that tag anymore.
resolution: Queried GitLab API for all pipelines stuck in pending state
Identified the deprecated arm64-legacy tag as the common cause across affected pipelines
Bulk-updated .gitlab-ci.yml tag references across affected projects via a scripted MR
Temporarily re-tagged two runners with arm64-legacy as a bridge while MRs merged
Cancelled and re-triggered all stuck pipelines
preventive_actions: Deprecate runner tags with a transition period where both old and new tags are honored
Add a CI linter that fails fast if a job references a non-existent runner tag
Alert when any pipeline remains pending for longer than 5 minutes
Maintain a central registry of valid runner tags referenced in onboarding docs
impact: 28 pipelines across 6 projects stuck for up to 1.5 hours, delaying merges and deployments.
lesson_learned: Runner tag migrations need a deprecation window, not a hard cutover, since job definitions live in many repos outside CI infra's direct control.

title: Terraform Apply Failing After Provider Version Drift
description: terraform apply began failing with schema validation errors on the aws provider after a CI runner image update silently pulled a newer major provider version than what the team had been using locally.
symptoms: terraform apply fails with 'Unsupported argument' on aws_instance resource
Error only occurs in CI, works locally for some developers
terraform version shows aws provider 5.x in CI vs 4.x expected
No changes made to .tf files recently
logs: 10:00:05 terraform Initializing provider plugins...
10:00:08 terraform Installing hashicorp/aws v5.42.0
10:00:20 terraform Error: Unsupported argument "instance_initiated_shutdown_behavior_legacy"
10:00:20 terraform on main.tf line 34, in resource "aws_instance" "app":

resolution: Identified the provider version mismatch via terraform version output in CI logs
Added an explicit required_providers version constraint pinning aws to ~> 4.0
Committed the .terraform.lock.hcl file to version control if not already tracked
Re-ran terraform init -upgrade=false to respect the lock file
Verified apply succeeded with the pinned provider version
preventive_actions: Always pin provider version constraints explicitly in required_providers blocks
Ensure .terraform.lock.hcl is committed and CI restores it before init
Cache the .terraform directory in CI to avoid unnecessary re-resolution
Add a scheduled job to test provider upgrades in an isolated branch before adopting
impact: Staging infrastructure changes blocked for 2 hours; no production impact.
lesson_learned: Unpinned provider versions turn routine CI image rebuilds into surprise breaking changes.

title: Ansible Playbook Idempotency Bug Causing Restart Loop
description: A scheduled Ansible playbook run intended to be a no-op configuration check instead restarted the nginx service on every managed host every night, causing brief but repeated service interruptions.
symptoms: nginx service restarts logged every night at 03:00
Brief 502 errors from load balancer during each restart
Ansible run reports 'changed' status for the nginx config task every single run
Config file content appears identical to previous run
logs: 03:20:01 ansible TASK [nginx : deploy config file]
03:20:02 ansible changed: [web-prod-01]
03:20:02 ansible changed: [web-prod-02]
03:20:03 ansible TASK [nginx : restart service]
03:20:04 ansible changed: [web-prod-01] => restarted nginx
03:20:05 systemd nginx.service: Deactivated successfully
03:20:06 systemd nginx.service: Started
root_cause: The Jinja2 template used a datetime.now() expression to stamp a 'generated at' comment in the nginx config file, so the rendered file content differed by a timestamp on every run, causing Ansible's template module to always report a change and trigger the notify-restart handler even when the meaningful configuration was unchanged.
resolution: Diffed the rendered config file across consecutive runs to spot the timestamp comment
Removed the dynamic timestamp from the Jinja2 template, replacing it with a static version string
Re-ran the playbook in check mode to confirm zero changes reported
Deployed the corrected template to all managed hosts
preventive_actions: Ban non-idempotent Jinja2 expressions (now(), random values) in managed templates via code review checklist
Run playbooks in --check --diff mode in CI to catch unexpected changes before merge
Add a canary host that runs the playbook first and alerts on unexpected 'changed' status
Document idempotency requirements in the Ansible style guide
impact: Brief service interruptions (2-4 seconds) on the web-prod fleet every night for an estimated 3 weeks before detection.
lesson_learned: Non-deterministic values in templates silently break idempotency and can cause recurring, hard-to-notice service disruptions.

title: EC2 Instance Retirement Caused Sudden Production Termination
description: A production EC2 instance running a stateful legacy order-processing service was terminated by AWS as part of a scheduled hardware retirement, and the service did not automatically recover because it was not part of an Auto Scaling Group.
symptoms: Instance state changes from running to terminated with no manual action
AWS Health Dashboard shows a scheduled retirement event 14 days prior
logs: 04:00:00 aws-health Instance i-0abc123def scheduled retirement event executed
04:00:01 ec2 Instance i-0abc123def state changed: running -> shutting-down
04:00:45 ec2 Instance i-0abc123def state changed: shutting-down -> terminated
04:01:10 elb Target i-0abc123def failed health check, removed from target group
04:01:10 elb 0 healthy targets in target group order-service-tg
root_cause: AWS had notified the account 14 days earlier of a scheduled instance retirement due to underlying hardware degradation, but the notification was not routed to the owning team's alerting channel, and the instance was a standalone EC2 host running a legacy service outside any Auto Scaling Group, so nothing launched a replacement when AWS terminated it.
resolution: Identified the termination cause via AWS Health Dashboard and CloudTrail
Launched a new EC2 instance from the last AMI snapshot
Reattached the persisted EBS data volume from the terminated instance
Registered the new instance with the target group
Verified order-service health checks passing and processing resumed
preventive_actions: Route AWS Health Dashboard scheduled-event notifications to the on-call alerting channel
Migrate legacy standalone EC2 services into an Auto Scaling Group with a launch template
Inventory all non-ASG production EC2 instances and prioritize migration
Set up automated EBS snapshots on a schedule for stateful instances
impact: order-service was fully unavailable for 22 minutes; approximately 40 orders required manual reprocessing.
lesson_learned: AWS scheduled retirement notices are a real deadline, not a formality — any instance outside auto-recovery infrastructure needs a manual response plan.

title: Lambda Concurrency Limit Throttling Checkout Requests
description: During a marketing-driven traffic surge, the checkout-processing Lambda function began returning HTTP 429 errors as invocations hit the account's regional concurrency limit, which was shared with several unrelated functions.
symptoms: API Gateway returning 429 Too Many Requests
CloudWatch shows Lambda Throttles metric spiking
ConcurrentExecutions metric flatlined at account limit of 1000
Other unrelated Lambda functions in the same account also throttling
logs: 18:28:00 cloudwatch checkout-lambda Invocations: 850/min
18:29:10 cloudwatch checkout-lambda ConcurrentExecutions: 1000 (account limit reached)
18:29:11 lambda Rate Exceeded: reserved concurrent execution limit exceeded
18:29:12 api-gateway 429 Too Many Requests returned to client
18:29:15 cloudwatch unrelated-function-batch-job Throttles: 45 in last minute
root_cause: No function-level reserved concurrency had been configured for checkout-lambda, so it competed for capacity from the shared account-wide concurrency pool; an unrelated batch-processing function scaled up simultaneously during the same window and consumed enough concurrency headroom to push the account past its regional limit.
resolution: Identified the shared concurrency pool exhaustion via CloudWatch ConcurrentExecutions metric
Set reserved concurrency of 400 on checkout-lambda to guarantee capacity isolation
Requested an account-level concurrency limit increase from AWS support
Throttled the unrelated batch job's invocation rate temporarily
Monitored throttle metrics until fully cleared
preventive_actions: Set reserved concurrency on all customer-facing Lambda functions
Request a higher account concurrency limit proactively ahead of known high-traffic events
Separate high-priority and batch workloads into different AWS accounts or use provisioned concurrency
Alert on Lambda Throttles metric exceeding zero for any customer-facing function
impact: Approximately 6% of checkout attempts failed with 429 errors over a 25-minute window during peak marketing traffic.
lesson_learned: Shared account-level concurrency limits mean one function's traffic spike can silently throttle an unrelated critical function.

title: ECS Task OOMKilled Due to Memory Reservation Mismatch
description: image-resizer ECS tasks were repeatedly killed and restarted because the task definition's soft memory reservation was set far lower than the container's actual peak usage during large batch image processing jobs.
symptoms: ECS console shows tasks stopped with reason 'OutOfMemoryError: Container killed'
Task restarts every 3-5 minutes during batch processing windows
ECS agent logs show container exceeding memory limit
CloudWatch container memory utilization spikes to 100% before each kill
logs: 12:00:00 ecs-agent Task arn:...:task/image-resizer/abc123 started
12:02:30 ecs-agent Container memory utilization: 480MB / 512MB
12:03:10 ecs-agent Container memory utilization: 512MB / 512MB
12:03:12 ecs-agent Container killed: OutOfMemoryError
12:03:15 ecs-agent Task stopped, reason: OutOfMemoryError: Container killed due to memory usage
root_cause: The task definition specified a hard memory limit of 512MB based on typical single-image processing, but a recent feature added batch processing of up to 20 images per invocation, multiplying peak memory usage well beyond the configured limit.
resolution: Reviewed CloudWatch Container Insights to confirm actual peak memory usage during batch jobs (around 1.8GB)
Updated the ECS task definition memory limit from 512MB to 2048MB
Adjusted the task's CPU allocation proportionally per Fargate sizing rules
Redeployed the service and monitored memory utilization during the next batch window
preventive_actions: Add CloudWatch Container Insights memory alerts at 80% of the configured limit
Load test any new batch-processing feature against existing resource limits before release
Document resource sizing assumptions in the task definition alongside the config
Review task definition resource limits quarterly against actual usage trends
impact: Batch image processing jobs failed and retried repeatedly for about 1 hour, delaying content publishing.
lesson_learned: A feature change that alters workload shape (single item to batch) invalidates prior resource sizing assumptions.

title: EKS IRSA Misconfiguration Causing S3 Access Denied
description: report-generator pods began failing to write generated reports to S3 with AccessDenied errors after a Kubernetes namespace migration inadvertently changed the service account used by the pods, breaking the IAM Role for Service Accounts (IRSA) binding.
symptoms: Application logs show S3 AccessDenied (403) on PutObject
Pods running under a different service account than before migration
IAM role trust policy still references the old namespace
No changes made to IAM policy permissions themselves
logs: 09:15:02 report-generator ERROR PutObject failed: AccessDenied: User arn:aws:sts::...:assumed-role/eks-node-role is not authorized
09:15:03 report-generator Falling back to node instance role, which lacks S3 permissions
09:15:05 kubelet ServiceAccount used: default (expected: report-generator-sa)
09:16:00 report-generator ERROR Retrying PutObject, attempt 3 of 3, giving up
root_cause: A namespace migration moved the report-generator Deployment from the 'reports' namespace to 'analytics' without updating the Deployment's serviceAccountName field, so pods fell back to the default service account which has no IAM role annotation, causing AWS SDK calls to fall back to the node's IAM role rather than the intended IRSA role with S3 permissions.
resolution: Traced the AccessDenied error to the pod's assumed identity via aws sts get-caller-identity from inside the pod
Confirmed the Deployment was missing the correct serviceAccountName after migration
Updated the Deployment manifest to reference report-generator-sa in the analytics namespace
Updated the IAM role trust policy condition to match the new namespace/service-account subject
Rolled out the corrected Deployment and verified successful S3 writes
preventive_actions: Add a pre-migration checklist item to verify serviceAccountName and IRSA bindings
Use OPA/Gatekeeper policy to reject Deployments missing an explicit serviceAccountName in namespaces requiring IRSA
Add integration test that verifies S3 write access as part of deployment smoke tests
Document IRSA trust policy subject format clearly in the migration runbook
impact: Report generation failed for all reports over a 50-minute window; reports queued and were regenerated after the fix.
lesson_learned: Namespace migrations silently break IRSA if the service account binding isn't explicitly carried over, since Kubernetes falls back to 'default' without erroring.

title: Overly Permissive IAM Policy Enabled Unauthorized Resource Creation
description: An IAM policy attached to a CI/CD deployment role was found to grant iam:* and ec2:* wildcard permissions, and a compromised CI runner credential was used to spin up unauthorized EC2 instances for cryptocurrency mining.
symptoms: Unexpected EC2 instances (c5.24xlarge) appearing in an unused AWS region
Billing alert for anomalous EC2 spend
CloudTrail shows RunInstances calls from CI deployment role outside business hours
logs: 02:35:10 cloudtrail AssumeRole ci-deploy-role from unusual source IP
02:36:00 cloudtrail RunInstances x12 c5.24xlarge in ap-southeast-1
02:36:05 guardduty Finding: CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B on i-0f1e2d3c
02:40:00 billing-alert Anomalous EC2 spend detected: +$4,200/hr projected
root_cause: The CI/CD deployment role's IAM policy had been granted iam:* and ec2:* wildcard actions months earlier as a quick fix to unblock a deployment issue and was never scoped down; a leaked CI runner access key (from an unrelated third-party log aggregator breach) was used by an attacker to assume this over-privileged role and launch mining instances.
resolution: Immediately terminated all unauthorized EC2 instances identified via GuardDuty and CloudTrail
Revoked and rotated the compromised CI runner access key
Disabled the ci-deploy-role pending policy review
Rewrote the IAM policy following least-privilege, scoping to only required actions and resource ARNs
Enabled AWS Config rules to detect wildcard IAM policies going forward
preventive_actions: Enforce least-privilege IAM policies via automated policy linting in CI (e.g., IAM Access Analyzer)
Rotate CI/CD credentials on a regular schedule and after any third-party vendor incident
Enable GuardDuty and route findings to a paged on-call security channel
Require MFA or short-lived credentials (OIDC federation) instead of long-lived CI access keys
impact: Unauthorized compute incurred approximately $1,100 in cloud spend before termination; no customer data was accessed.
lesson_learned: Wildcard IAM policies added as a 'temporary' fix are a standing risk — every over-privileged role is a bigger blast radius for any future credential leak.

Impact: Unauthorized compute incurred approximately $1,100 in cloud spend before termination; no customer data was accessed. Resolution time: 1 hour 10 minutes.

title: S3 Bucket Policy Misconfiguration Exposed Customer Data Publicly
description: A Terraform change intended to allow a partner service to read a specific S3 prefix instead applied a bucket-wide public-read policy due to an incorrect resource ARN pattern, exposing customer export files to the internet for several hours before detection.
symptoms: S3 bucket publicly listable via unauthenticated HTTP request
AWS Trusted Advisor flags bucket as 'Open Access'
Access logs show GET requests from unrecognized external IPs
Security scanner (external) reports the bucket in a public exposure report
logs: 05:00:00 terraform apply Applying aws_s3_bucket_policy.data_exports
05:00:12 terraform apply Apply complete. 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed
07:45:00 external-scanner Public S3 bucket detected: data-exports-prod
07:46:00 s3-access-log GET /customer_export_4471.csv 200 (unauthenticated, IP 203.0.113.44)
root_cause: The Terraform bucket policy used a resource pattern of arn:aws:s3:::data-exports-prod/* intended to be scoped further by a condition block, but the condition block referenced an incorrect variable name that silently evaluated to an always-true wildcard, resulting in unrestricted public read access to every object in the bucket.
resolution: Immediately applied an emergency bucket policy to block all public access (S3 Block Public Access)
Identified and fixed the incorrect condition variable in the Terraform module
Audited S3 access logs to determine what objects were actually accessed during the exposure window
Notified affected customers per data breach disclosure policy
Re-applied the corrected, properly scoped policy and verified via aws s3api get-bucket-policy
preventive_actions: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the account level as a default guardrail
Add automated policy-as-code scanning (e.g., Checkov, tfsec) to CI for all S3 bucket policy changes
Require security team review for any Terraform change touching bucket policies or ACLs
Set up continuous public-bucket monitoring via AWS Config and GuardDuty S3 protection
impact: Customer export files were publicly accessible for approximately 2 hours 45 minutes; confirmed unauthorized access to 14 files, triggering customer notification.
lesson_learned: A single mistyped Terraform variable in a policy condition can silently turn a scoped grant into a public one — policy-as-code changes need automated scanning, not just code review.

title: CloudFront Cache Invalidation Storm Overloading Origin
description: A deployment script bug issued a full-path cache invalidation (/*) on every single deploy instead of only changed assets, and back-to-back deploys during a release window caused a flood of origin requests that overwhelmed the origin web servers.
symptoms: Origin server CPU and connection count spiking to capacity
CloudFront cache hit ratio dropping from 98% to 20%
Origin 5xx errors returned through CloudFront to end users
Multiple /* invalidation requests visible in CloudFront invalidation history within a short window
logs: 13:00:00 deploy-script Creating CloudFront invalidation for paths: ["/*"]
13:00:05 cloudfront Invalidation IN3X7Y9 created, status InProgress
13:04:00 deploy-script Creating CloudFront invalidation for paths: ["/*"]
13:08:00 origin-alb Origin CPUUtilization: 96%
13:09:00 origin-alb Target 5xx count: 340 in last minute
root_cause: The deploy script's cache-busting logic was written to always invalidate /* as a 'safe default' rather than computing the actual set of changed asset paths, and three deploys were triggered in quick succession during a release, each forcing CloudFront to bypass cache for every request until repopulated, which the origin fleet was not sized to handle simultaneously.
resolution: Identified the invalidation pattern as the trigger via CloudFront invalidation history
Paused further deploys to stop additional invalidations
Temporarily scaled up the origin ALB target group to absorb the cache-miss load
Waited for CloudFront cache to naturally repopulate and hit ratio to recover
Fixed the deploy script to invalidate only changed asset paths going forward
preventive_actions: Replace /* invalidations with targeted path invalidation based on the actual build diff
Use versioned/hashed asset filenames to avoid needing invalidation for most deploys
Rate-limit or queue deploy-triggered invalidations to prevent overlapping storms
Set origin fleet auto-scaling policies based on cache-miss-driven load patterns, not just steady-state traffic
impact: Elevated error rates and slow page loads for end users for approximately 15 minutes during the release window.
lesson_learned: Broad cache invalidation is a 'safe default' for correctness but an origin-overload risk at scale — targeted invalidation and content hashing avoid the tradeoff entirely.

title: Redis Cluster Failover Caused Keyspace Split and Session Loss
description: During a Redis Cluster master node failure, an automatic failover promoted a replica that had not fully synced the latest writes, resulting in a brief keyspace split where some user session data written just before the failure was permanently lost.
symptoms: Users unexpectedly logged out and required to re-authenticate
Redis INFO shows master_repl_offset mismatch between old and new master
Application logs show session key not found errors for recently created sessions
Redis Sentinel logs show failover promoted replica-2 despite lower replication offset than replica-1
logs: 15:28:00 redis-sentinel +sdown master redis-master-1 192.168.10.5:6379
15:28:05 redis-sentinel +failover-state-select-slave master redis-master-1
15:28:06 redis-sentinel +selected-slave slave 192.168.10.7:6379 (replica-2)
15:28:10 redis-sentinel +promoted-slave slave 192.168.10.7:6379
15:29:00 app-logs WARN Session key sess:8842f1 not found, forcing re-auth
root_cause: Sentinel's default replica selection did not account for replication offset lag between candidates precisely enough under the specific network partition pattern that occurred, selecting a replica (replica-2) with a slightly stale replication offset over a more current one, so writes acknowledged by the old master in its last moments were never propagated to the promoted replica and were lost.
resolution: Confirmed data loss scope was limited to writes in the last ~2 seconds before failover
Communicated to affected users via forced re-authentication rather than silent errors
Manually reconciled critical session state from application-level audit logs where possible
Tuned Sentinel configuration (min-replicas-to-write, min-replicas-max-lag) to reduce acknowledgment of writes without sufficient replica confirmation
preventive_actions: Configure min-replicas-to-write and min-replicas-max-lag to avoid acknowledging writes with insufficient replication
Consider Redis with WAIT command or synchronous replication for session data specifically
Move session storage to a data store with stronger consistency guarantees if session loss is unacceptable
Add monitoring for replication offset delta between master and replicas as an early warning
impact: Approximately 3,200 active user sessions were invalidated, requiring re-login; no other data affected.
lesson_learned: Redis's default async replication trades consistency for availability — anything session-critical needs explicit write-acknowledgment tuning or a different store.

title: PostgreSQL Replication Lag From Long-Running Autovacuum
description: A long-running autovacuum process on a heavily-written orders table held resources long enough to delay WAL shipping, causing the read replica to fall over 10 minutes behind and serve stale order status to the customer-facing order-tracking page.
symptoms: ReplicationLag metric on read replica climbing steadily past 600 seconds
pg_stat_activity shows autovacuum worker running for over 40 minutes on orders table
Customers reporting order status pages show outdated 'processing' state after delivery
WAL sender process showing increased lag in pg_stat_replication
logs: 01:00:00 postgres autovacuum: processing database "orders_db"
01:00:00 postgres autovacuum: VACUUM ANALYZE public.orders (dead tuples: 2.1M)
01:15:00 postgres autovacuum worker still running on orders table (14 min)
01:35:00 pg_stat_replication replica-1 replay_lag: 612 seconds
01:40:00 app-logs order-tracking page serving data from replica with stale status
root_cause: The orders table had accumulated a large number of dead tuples from frequent updates without autovacuum tuning adjusted for its write volume, so when autovacuum finally triggered it needed to scan and clean an unusually large number of dead rows in one long pass, consuming I/O and lock resources that delayed WAL generation and shipping to the replica.
resolution: Identified the long-running autovacuum process via pg_stat_activity
Allowed the autovacuum to complete rather than cancelling it mid-run (cancelling would only delay cleanup further)
Temporarily routed order-tracking reads to the primary instance to serve current data
Once replication lag cleared, routed reads back to the replica
Tuned autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor lower for the orders table to trigger more frequent, smaller vacuum passes
preventive_actions: Tune per-table autovacuum settings for high-churn tables instead of relying on global defaults
Monitor pg_stat_user_tables dead tuple counts and alert before they become vacuum-storm-sized
Add application-level replica lag awareness with fallback to primary for staleness-sensitive reads
Schedule a maintenance window for a manual VACUUM on the orders table if backlog grows too large
impact: Order-tracking page showed stale status for up to 12 minutes for customers relying on the read replica; no data loss.
lesson_learned: Autovacuum defaults tuned for average tables can turn into a multi-minute resource hog on high-churn tables — per-table tuning matters at scale.

title: MySQL Table Lock Contention Backing Up Query Queue
description: A large, unindexed ALTER TABLE run during business hours took an exclusive metadata lock on the inventory table, blocking all reads and writes and causing a rapidly growing backlog of queued application queries.
symptoms: Application requests to inventory-service timing out after 30 seconds
SHOW PROCESSLIST shows dozens of queries in 'Waiting for table metadata lock' state
MySQL connection pool exhausted with queued waiting connections
ALTER TABLE query itself running for over 8 minutes
logs: 11:20:00 mysql Query: ALTER TABLE inventory ADD COLUMN warehouse_zone VARCHAR(50)
11:20:05 mysql 12 queries now in state 'Waiting for table metadata lock'
11:22:00 mysql 58 queries now in state 'Waiting for table metadata lock'
11:22:00 app-logs Connection pool exhausted, 0 available connections
11:28:00 mysql ALTER TABLE inventory ... completed, 480.2 sec
root_cause: The ALTER TABLE statement was run directly against the production primary during business hours without using an online schema change tool, and because it required an exclusive metadata lock for the full duration of the table rebuild (8 minutes on a large table), every subsequent read and write query queued behind it, rapidly exhausting the application's connection pool.
resolution: Identified the blocking ALTER TABLE via SHOW PROCESSLIST and information_schema.innodb_trx
Could not safely kill the ALTER mid-run without risking table corruption, so waited for completion while monitoring
Once complete, connection pool queue drained rapidly to normal wait times
Documented the incident and the correct tool to use for future schema changes
preventive_actions: Require all production schema changes to use an online DDL tool (e.g., gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change)
Schedule any unavoidable blocking schema changes during a low-traffic maintenance window
Add a pre-deployment check that flags direct ALTER TABLE statements against production databases
Set a reasonable lock_wait_timeout so blocked queries fail fast and surface visibly instead of queuing silently
impact: inventory-service was effectively unavailable for 8 minutes; order processing delayed for affected customers during that window.
lesson_learned: Any schema change on a large, actively-queried production table needs an online DDL tool — direct ALTER TABLE is an outage waiting to happen.

title: MongoDB Missing Index Causing Full Collection Scan CPU Spike
description: A new search filter field was added to the user-search feature without a corresponding index, causing every query using that filter to perform a full collection scan and driving primary node CPU to sustained 100%.
symptoms: MongoDB primary CPU utilization sustained at 100% for over 20 minutes
user-search queries taking 8-12 seconds instead of typical 50ms
mongod logs show COLLSCAN in query plans for the new filter
Other queries against the same collection also slowing due to CPU contention
logs: 17:00:00 mongod [conn4821] query users.profiles planSummary: COLLSCAN, took 8420ms
17:00:05 mongod [conn4822] query users.profiles planSummary: COLLSCAN, took 9120ms
17:01:00 mongostat CPU: 100% Primary node
17:02:00 app-logs user-search request timeout after 10000ms
root_cause: A recent release added filtering by a new 'preferred_language' field to the user-search API, but the corresponding index was never created on that field, so MongoDB's query planner fell back to a full collection scan on a collection with over 40 million documents for every search request using the new filter.
resolution: Identified the COLLSCAN pattern via mongod query logs and explain() output
Created a background index on the preferred_language field to avoid blocking reads/writes during creation
Monitored index build progress and CPU utilization during the build
Verified query plans switched to IXSCAN and latency returned to baseline once the index completed
preventive_actions: Require an index review as part of code review for any new query filter field
Add a CI/staging check that runs explain() on new query patterns and fails on COLLSCAN for large collections
Enable MongoDB's slow query profiler in production with alerting on COLLSCAN occurrences
Document indexing requirements in the API contribution guide
impact: user-search latency degraded for all users for approximately 25 minutes; some requests timed out entirely.
lesson_learned: A new query filter field is a schema change in disguise — it needs the same indexing review as an actual schema migration.

title: Elasticsearch Shard Allocation Failure From Disk Watermark Breach
description: Several Elasticsearch data nodes crossed the high disk watermark threshold due to rapid log ingestion growth, causing the cluster to stop allocating new shards and forcing indices into a degraded yellow/red health state.
symptoms: Cluster health status shows yellow, then red for some indices
New log documents rejected with 'disk usage exceeded flood-stage watermark'
GET _cluster/allocation/explain shows shard allocation blocked due to disk space
Kibana dashboards showing gaps in recent log data
logs: 06:30:00 elasticsearch [node-data-3] high disk watermark [90%] exceeded
06:31:00 elasticsearch Rerouting shards away from node-data-3
06:35:00 elasticsearch [node-data-3] flood-stage disk watermark [95%] exceeded, enforcing read-only-allow-delete
06:35:01 elasticsearch index [logs-2026.02.24] blocked with read_only_allow_delete=true
06:36:00 app-logs Bulk index request rejected: cluster_block_exception
root_cause: A new high-volume microservice began emitting significantly more verbose debug-level logs than anticipated, and index lifecycle management (ILM) rollover/deletion policies had not been updated to account for the increased ingestion rate, so old indices weren't rolled off fast enough to keep pace with disk consumption on the data nodes.
resolution: Identified the disk watermark breach via cluster health and node stats APIs
Manually deleted the oldest, least-critical log indices to reclaim disk space below the flood-stage threshold
Removed the read_only_allow_delete block once disk usage dropped below the high watermark
Reduced the offending microservice's log verbosity from DEBUG to INFO as an immediate mitigation
Verified indexing resumed and cluster health returned to green
preventive_actions: Tighten ILM rollover and retention policies to match actual ingestion growth trends
Add disk usage alerts at 75% and 85% well before the built-in 90%/95% watermarks trigger
Set per-service log volume budgets and alert when a service exceeds its expected baseline
Add more data nodes or increase storage proactively ahead of known high-growth periods
impact: Log ingestion was degraded or blocked for approximately 35 minutes, creating gaps in observability during that window.
lesson_learned: ILM retention policies need to be revisited whenever ingestion volume changes meaningfully, not just set once at initial cluster setup.
