Description: Several Elasticsearch data nodes crossed the high disk watermark threshold due to rapid log ingestion growth, causing the cluster to stop allocating new shards and forcing indices into a degraded yellow/red health state. Symptoms observed: Cluster health status shows yellow, then red for some indices; New log documents rejected with 'disk usage exceeded flood-stage watermark'; GET _cluster/allocation/explain shows shard allocation blocked due to disk space; Kibana dashboards showing gaps in recent log data. Representative log/alert lines: 06:30:00 elasticsearch [node-data-3] high disk watermark [90%] exceeded | 06:31:00 elasticsearch Rerouting shards away from node-data-3 | 06:35:00 elasticsearch [node-data-3] flood-stage disk watermark [95%] exceeded, enforcing read-only-allow-delete | 06:35:01 elasticsearch index [logs-2026.02.24] blocked with read_only_allow_delete=true | 06:36:00 app-logs Bulk index request rejected: cluster_block_exception. Affected components: Elasticsearch data nodes, log-search index cluster, log ingestion pipeline. Root cause: A new high-volume microservice began emitting significantly more verbose debug-level logs than anticipated, and index lifecycle management (ILM) rollover/deletion policies had not been updated to account for the increased ingestion rate, so old indices weren't rolled off fast enough to keep pace with disk consumption on the data nodes. Resolution steps: Identified the disk watermark breach via cluster health and node stats APIs; Manually deleted the oldest, least-critical log indices to reclaim disk space below the flood-stage threshold; Removed the read_only_allow_delete block once disk usage dropped below the high watermark; Reduced the offending microservice's log verbosity from DEBUG to INFO as an immediate mitigation; Verified indexing resumed and cluster health returned to green. Preventive actions: Tighten ILM rollover and retention policies to match actual ingestion growth trends; Add disk usage alerts at 75% and 85% well before the built-in 90%/95% watermarks trigger; Set per-service log volume budgets and alert when a service exceeds its expected baseline; Add more data nodes or increase storage proactively ahead of known high-growth periods. Impact: Log ingestion was degraded or blocked for approximately 35 minutes, creating gaps in observability during that window. Lesson learned: ILM retention policies need to be revisited whenever ingestion volume changes meaningfully, not just set once at initial cluster setup. Resolution time: 35 minutes.

title: Kafka Consumer Group Rebalance Storm Halting Message Processing
description: A misconfigured consumer session timeout caused the event-processor consumer group to enter a continuous rebalance loop after a deploy, during which no partitions were being actively consumed and message lag grew unbounded.
symptoms: Consumer lag climbing continuously across all partitions
Kafka broker logs show repeated group rebalances for group event-processor-group
Application logs show consumers joining and immediately being revoked
No messages being processed despite consumers reporting as running
logs: 14:45:00 kafka [GroupCoordinator] Preparing to rebalance group event-processor-group
14:45:03 kafka [GroupCoordinator] Stabilized group event-processor-group generation 47
14:45:35 kafka [GroupCoordinator] Member consumer-3 removed from group, reason: session timeout
14:45:36 kafka [GroupCoordinator] Preparing to rebalance group event-processor-group generation 48
14:46:10 kafka [GroupCoordinator] Preparing to rebalance group event-processor-group generation 49
root_cause: A deploy changed the message processing logic to include a synchronous call to a slow external enrichment API, extending average processing time per poll well beyond the configured max.poll.interval.ms, so the broker kept assuming consumers had died and evicting them, triggering a rebalance every time a new consumer tried to resume and immediately exceeded the interval again.
resolution: Identified the rebalance loop pattern via broker GroupCoordinator logs
Rolled back the deploy that introduced the synchronous external API call
Confirmed consumer group stabilized after rollback (single rebalance, then stable)
Monitored consumer lag draining back to near-zero as backlog was processed
preventive_actions: Increase max.poll.interval.ms appropriately for any processing logic with external calls, or move slow calls to async processing
Add a pre-deploy check that measures average processing time per message against the configured poll interval
Alert on consumer group rebalance rate exceeding a threshold (e.g., more than 3 rebalances in 5 minutes)
Prefer async/batched enrichment calls over synchronous per-message external API calls in consumer logic
impact: Message processing was effectively halted for 30 minutes, delaying downstream order fulfillment events; all messages eventually processed with no data loss.
lesson_learned: Any change that slows per-message processing time needs to be checked against consumer poll interval settings, or it silently turns into a rebalance storm.

title: RabbitMQ Queue Mirroring Failure Causing Message Loss
description: A network blip between RabbitMQ cluster nodes caused a mirrored queue to lose synchronization, and when the queue's master node was subsequently restarted for a routine patch, an unsynchronized mirror was promoted, permanently dropping unacknowledged messages.
symptoms: order-events-queue message count drops unexpectedly after node restart
RabbitMQ management UI shows mirror was 'unsynchronised' before promotion
Consumers report missing expected order events downstream
Cluster logs show partition detected and healed shortly before the incident
logs: 08:55:00 rabbitmq Node rabbit@node-2 detected network partition with rabbit@node-1
08:55:30 rabbitmq Partition healed, rabbit@node-2 rejoined cluster
08:56:00 rabbitmq Mirror for queue order-events-queue on node-2 is unsynchronised
09:00:00 rabbitmq Node rabbit@node-1 stopping for maintenance
09:00:05 rabbitmq Promoting unsynchronised mirror on rabbit@node-2 for queue order-events-queue
root_cause: The queue's mirroring policy did not set ha-promote-on-shutdown to 'when-synced', so when the master node was intentionally stopped for maintenance while its mirror was still catching up from an earlier brief network partition, RabbitMQ promoted the out-of-sync mirror anyway rather than refusing promotion, silently dropping the messages that had not yet replicated.
resolution: Identified the unsynchronised mirror promotion via RabbitMQ cluster status logs
Audited downstream order-fulfillment logs to identify which order events were missing
Manually replayed the missing order events from the upstream source-of-truth database where recoverable
Updated the queue mirroring policy to set ha-promote-on-shutdown=when-synced
Rescheduled the remaining maintenance restarts to occur only after confirming full mirror sync
preventive_actions: Set ha-promote-on-shutdown=when-synced on all mirrored queues carrying critical messages
Add pre-maintenance checks that verify mirror sync status before restarting any cluster node
Alert immediately on any queue mirror entering an unsynchronised state
Consider migrating critical event queues to quorum queues, which have stronger consistency guarantees than classic mirrored queues
impact: Approximately 140 order events were lost and required manual reconciliation from source data; some downstream processing delayed by hours.
lesson_learned: Classic mirrored queues can silently promote an out-of-sync mirror unless explicitly configured not to — quorum queues avoid this failure mode entirely.

title: NGINX Worker Crash From Malformed Regex in Location Block
description: A newly deployed NGINX configuration with a catastrophic-backtracking regular expression in a location block caused worker processes to hang and eventually crash under real traffic patterns, resulting in widespread 502 errors.
symptoms: 502 Bad Gateway errors returned to a growing share of clients
NGINX worker processes showing high CPU (single core pegged at 100%)
New worker processes spawned and immediately pegged after old ones killed
Issue only appears under production traffic, not in staging smoke tests
logs: 10:10:00 nginx worker process 8821 CPU: 100% (single core)
10:10:05 nginx [alert] worker process 8821 exited on signal 9 (killed)
10:10:06 nginx worker process 8834 started
10:10:40 nginx worker process 8834 CPU: 100% (single core)
10:11:00 nginx upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading response header from upstream
root_cause: A newly added location block used a regular expression with nested quantifiers to match certain API paths, which under specific real-world query string patterns (not present in staging test traffic) triggered catastrophic backtracking, causing the matching worker thread to consume 100% CPU for an extended period and eventually be killed by the OS or watchdog.
resolution: Identified the CPU-pegged worker pattern and correlated it with recent config deploy timing
Reviewed the new location block and identified the vulnerable regex pattern
Rolled back to the previous NGINX configuration immediately to restore service
Rewrote the regex using a non-backtracking, more specific pattern
Load tested the corrected config against production-like traffic samples before redeploying
preventive_actions: Ban nested-quantifier regex patterns in NGINX config via a linting tool (e.g., regex complexity analysis)
Capture and replay real production traffic samples in staging load tests, not just synthetic smoke tests
Set a hard CPU watchdog alert on individual NGINX worker processes
Require config changes touching location block regexes to go through an extra review step
impact: Approximately 30% of API requests failed with 502 errors during the 18-minute incident window before rollback.
lesson_learned: Regex catastrophic backtracking is invisible in staging until the right input pattern appears in production traffic — regex complexity needs static analysis, not just functional testing.

title: HAProxy Health Check Misconfiguration Routing Traffic to Unhealthy Backend
description: An HAProxy health check configured against a lightweight /ping endpoint continued reporting backend servers as healthy even after their actual application logic had deadlocked, causing HAProxy to keep routing real user traffic to servers that couldn't process it.
symptoms: HAProxy stats page shows all backend servers as UP (green)
Real user requests to /checkout returning no response until client-side timeout
Backend application logs show thread pool exhausted, but /ping endpoint still responding
Error rate rising steadily despite HAProxy reporting a fully healthy backend pool
logs: 16:00:00 haproxy Server backend/app-3 is UP, reason: Layer7 check passed (GET /ping)
16:02:00 app-3-logs WARN Thread pool exhausted, 0 available workers
16:02:05 haproxy Server backend/app-3 is UP, reason: Layer7 check passed (GET /ping)
16:05:00 client-logs Request to /checkout timed out after 30000ms
16:05:00 haproxy Server backend/app-3 is UP, reason: Layer7 check passed (GET /ping)
root_cause: The /ping health check endpoint was implemented as a static, hardcoded 200 OK response handled by a dedicated lightweight thread outside the main application thread pool, so it kept responding successfully even after the main request-handling thread pool had fully deadlocked due to a downstream dependency hang, giving HAProxy a false signal of backend health.
resolution: Identified the discrepancy between HAProxy's healthy status and actual application failure via correlated logs
Manually removed app-3 from the HAProxy backend pool to stop routing traffic to it
Restarted the app-3 application process to clear the deadlocked thread pool
Re-added app-3 to the pool once verified healthy under real request load, not just /ping
preventive_actions: Rewrite the health check endpoint to exercise the actual application thread pool (e.g., a lightweight but real request through the main handler path)
Add a deep health check in addition to the shallow one, checked less frequently but weighted more heavily
Monitor real request success rate independently of HAProxy's own health check status as a cross-check
Add thread pool exhaustion alerting directly from the application
impact: A meaningful share of checkout requests failed or timed out for approximately 12 minutes before manual intervention.
lesson_learned: A shallow health check that bypasses the real request path can report 'healthy' on a server that's fully deadlocked for actual traffic — health checks need to exercise the real code path.

title: Istio Sidecar Injection Failure Breaking mTLS Between Services
description: A namespace label was accidentally removed during a Kubernetes namespace update, disabling automatic Istio sidecar injection for newly deployed pods and causing mTLS handshake failures between mesh-enabled and non-mesh services.
symptoms: New pods deployed without an istio-proxy sidecar container
Connection refused / mTLS handshake failed errors between services
istioctl proxy-status shows affected pods missing from the mesh entirely
Only pods deployed after the namespace update affected; older pods still running fine
logs: 08:20:00 kubectl apply Namespace payments-prod updated (label istio-injection removed)
08:21:00 kubelet Pod payments-api-7f9c-x1 created without sidecar container
08:22:00 envoy [upstream connect error] connection reset before headers, TLS error
08:22:01 app-logs payments-api Failed to connect to inventory-api: connection refused
08:23:00 istioctl proxy-status payments-api-7f9c-x1 NOT IN MESH
root_cause: An unrelated namespace metadata update overwrote the full labels map instead of patching a single key, inadvertently removing the istio-injection=enabled label required by the Istio mutating webhook to auto-inject the Envoy sidecar, so new pods in that namespace were deployed without the sidecar and could not participate in the mesh's mTLS-secured communication.
resolution: Identified missing sidecars via istioctl proxy-status and kubectl describe pod
Confirmed the namespace label was missing via kubectl get namespace payments-prod --show-labels
Restored the istio-injection=enabled label on the namespace
Triggered a rollout restart of affected Deployments to get pods recreated with sidecar injection
Verified mTLS connectivity restored via istioctl proxy-status and successful service calls
preventive_actions: Use kubectl label (patch) instead of full metadata replacement for namespace label changes
Add an admission policy or CI check that verifies required namespace labels before any namespace update is applied
Alert when istioctl proxy-status shows any pod in a mesh-enabled namespace as NOT IN MESH
Document namespace labels as protected/critical configuration requiring extra review
impact: payments-api could not reach mesh-internal dependencies for 15 minutes, blocking a portion of payment processing.
lesson_learned: A single accidentally-dropped namespace label can silently remove pods from the service mesh — namespace metadata changes deserve the same scrutiny as application config changes.

title: Prometheus Remote Write Buffer Overflow Dropping Metrics
description: A network slowdown to the long-term storage backend caused Prometheus's remote write queue to fill faster than it could drain, and once the in-memory buffer overflowed, several minutes of metric samples were silently dropped rather than retried.
symptoms: Gaps appearing in Grafana dashboards for several minutes at a time
Prometheus remote write queue metrics show prometheus_remote_storage_samples_pending climbing toward the queue capacity
No alerts fired during the gap because the alerting rules themselves rely on the same metrics
logs: 19:00:00 prometheus remote_write queue: pending=8200/10000 shard=default
19:01:30 prometheus remote_write queue: pending=9950/10000 shard=default
19:02:00 prometheus remote_write samples dropped: 4200 (queue full)
19:02:00 prometheus remote_write remote storage endpoint latency p99: 4.8s (baseline: 200ms)
root_cause: The long-term storage backend (Thanos receive) was undergoing a rolling restart for a routine upgrade, causing elevated write latency on that side; Prometheus's remote write queue had a fixed capacity sized for normal-latency conditions, and once the queue filled during the elevated-latency window, newly scraped samples were dropped rather than blocked or retried, since Prometheus favors continuing to scrape over blocking on a slow remote endpoint.
resolution: Identified the dropped-samples counter increment correlating with the Thanos receive rolling restart window
Confirmed via Thanos receive logs that the restart caused a temporary write latency spike
Waited for the rolling restart to complete and remote write latency to return to baseline
Verified queue drained and dropped counter stopped incrementing
preventive_actions: Increase remote write queue capacity and configure a longer max_backoff to better absorb transient backend latency
Schedule long-term storage backend maintenance during low-traffic windows and communicate to observability consumers
Add an alert on prometheus_remote_storage_samples_dropped_total directly, independent of dashboards that depend on the same data
Consider a local buffering/replay mechanism for critical metrics during known maintenance windows
impact: Approximately 6 minutes of metric data across all monitored services was permanently lost, creating dashboard and historical analysis gaps.
lesson_learned: Monitoring the monitoring system matters — an alert that depends on the same pipeline it's meant to protect can't fire during that pipeline's own outage.

title: Grafana Dashboards Broken After Data Source Migration
description: After migrating the primary metrics data source from a self-hosted Prometheus instance to a managed Prometheus-compatible service, dozens of Grafana dashboards broke because the new data source used a different UID, and dashboards referenced the old UID directly rather than by name.
symptoms: Dashboards show 'Datasource not found' panel errors
Only dashboards imported via JSON (not created via UI) affected
New data source works correctly when manually selected in Explore view
Alerting rules referencing the old data source UID also failing to evaluate
logs: 10:00:00 grafana Datasource 'prometheus-managed' provisioned with uid=P8E80DA88DAA1F5A2
10:00:05 grafana Dashboard 'API Latency Overview' panel error: Datasource prometheus-old-uid-123 not found
10:00:06 grafana Dashboard 'Error Budget' panel error: Datasource prometheus-old-uid-123 not found

root_cause: The new managed Prometheus data source was provisioned with an auto-generated UID different from the old self-hosted instance's UID, and since many dashboards had been version-controlled and provisioned as JSON with the data source UID hardcoded (rather than using the 'default' data source or a templated variable), those dashboards lost their data binding entirely after the old data source was decommissioned.

title: Loki Ingester OOM From Oversized Log Line Ingestion
description: A misbehaving service began emitting multi-megabyte single log lines containing full stack traces with embedded binary data, and Loki's ingesters repeatedly OOMed while trying to buffer and chunk these oversized entries in memory.
symptoms: Loki ingester pods restarting every few minutes with OOMKilled status
Log queries for the affected service returning incomplete results
Ingester memory usage graphs show sawtooth pattern climbing rapidly before each crash
Promtail agent logs show 'entry too large' warnings being ignored/retried rather than dropped
logs: 21:00:00 promtail entry with timestamp ... size 4.2MB exceeds recommended size, forwarding anyway
21:00:05 loki-ingester Received entry size 4.2MB for stream {app="payment-worker"}
21:02:00 loki-ingester memstats: HeapAlloc 3.8GB / 4GB limit
21:02:30 loki-ingester OOMKilled
21:02:35 kubelet Container loki-ingester restarted (restart count: 14)
root_cause: A recent change to payment-worker's error handling began logging entire exception objects including embedded binary payloads as single log lines without truncation, producing multi-megabyte entries; Loki's ingester had no server-side max_line_size enforcement configured, so it accepted and attempted to buffer these oversized entries in memory, and enough of them arriving concurrently exhausted the ingester's memory limit.
resolution: Identified the oversized log entries via Promtail's size warning logs correlated with ingester OOM timing
Set Loki's limits_config max_line_size to reject entries above a reasonable threshold (256KB)
Restarted the ingester pods to clear the OOM state
Fixed payment-worker's logging code to truncate stack traces and exclude binary payloads from log output
preventive_actions: Enforce max_line_size at the Loki server (ingester) level, not just as a client-side warning
Add log line size limits to the shared application logging library used across services
Set memory-based alerts on Loki ingester pods before they reach OOM territory
Add a code review guideline against logging raw exception objects or binary data directly
impact: Log ingestion for multiple services (sharing ingesters) was intermittently degraded for approximately 25 minutes.
lesson_learned: A logging library that doesn't cap entry size is a shared-infrastructure risk — one misbehaving service can OOM the ingestion pipeline for everyone.

title: Helm Release Stuck After CRD Version Mismatch
description: A Helm upgrade for the cert-manager chart failed and left the release in a stuck 'pending-upgrade' state because the chart's new version required a CRD schema that hadn't been applied, and Helm's default CRD handling doesn't upgrade existing CRDs automatically.
symptoms: helm upgrade command hangs then fails with a timeout
kubectl get crd shows the old certificaterequests CRD schema still installed
New cert-manager pods crash-looping with CRD schema validation errors
logs: 13:30:00 helm Upgrading release cert-manager to chart version 1.18.0
13:30:45 helm Waiting for resources to become ready...
13:32:00 cert-manager-controller ERROR CRD schema validation failed: unknown field spec.revisionHistoryLimit
13:35:00 helm UPGRADE FAILED: timed out waiting for the condition
13:35:01 helm Release cert-manager status: pending-upgrade
root_cause: Helm intentionally does not upgrade or manage the lifecycle of CRDs after initial installation as a safety measure, but the cert-manager chart's new version shipped controller code expecting a newer CRD schema; since the CRDs were never manually updated as part of the upgrade process, the new controller pods failed schema validation against the stale CRD definitions.
resolution: Diagnosed the CRD/controller version mismatch via controller pod crash logs
Manually applied the updated CRD manifests from the new chart version using kubectl apply
Rolled back the stuck Helm release to the previous stable revision to restore a clean state: helm rollback cert-manager
Re-ran the upgrade after CRDs were current, which then completed successfully
Verified cert-manager pods running and certificate issuance functioning
preventive_actions: Always apply CRD manifest updates as an explicit, separate step before any Helm chart major/minor version upgrade that touches CRDs
Read the chart's upgrade notes/changelog for CRD-related breaking changes before upgrading
Use a CRD management tool (e.g., a dedicated CRD Helm chart or kubectl apply pipeline step) rather than relying on the parent chart
Test chart upgrades in staging with a CRD diff check before promoting to production
impact: cert-manager was in a degraded state in staging for 45 minutes; no production impact since staging caught the issue first.
lesson_learned: Helm's deliberate hands-off approach to CRD upgrades means every chart upgrade touching CRDs needs an explicit manual or scripted CRD-apply step.

title: PostgreSQL Connection Pool Exhaustion During Flash Sale
description: A large promotional flash sale generated nearly five times the normal checkout traffic. The Checkout Service relied on PgBouncer to manage PostgreSQL connections. As concurrent requests rapidly increased, the connection pool reached its configured limit, preventing new transactions from acquiring database connections. Customer checkouts failed while upstream services continued retrying requests, further increasing load on the database.
symptoms: Checkout latency increased from 280 ms to over 18 seconds

HikariCP - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms
Prometheus Alert: postgres_active_connections exceeded threshold
root_cause: Application autoscaling increased API pods without proportionally increasing database capacity. The larger number of application instances exhausted PgBouncer's client connection limit while several idle connections remained unreleased because of improper connection lifecycle management.

Applied temporary request rate limiting at API Gateway

Implement connection pool monitoring dashboards
Configure alerts at 80% pool utilization
Introduce read replicas for reporting workloads
impact: Approximately 31% of checkout requests failed for 17 minutes, affecting nearly 4,800 customer orders.

JVM heap usage steadily increased until multiple data nodes experienced prolonged garbage collection pauses, causing cluster instability, failed shard allocations, and intermittent search failures.

Shard allocation failed due to unavailable node
Prometheus Alert: elasticsearch_jvm_heap_used_percent exceeded 95
root_cause: Large bulk indexing operations generated excessive field data and query cache growth. Combined with inefficient aggregation queries, JVM heap became saturated, triggering repeated Full Garbage Collection cycles and temporary node instability.
preventive_actions: Monitor JVM heap usage continuously
Limit aggregation memory consumption
Schedule large indexing jobs during off-peak hours
Review field mapping strategy regularly
Implement predictive cluster capacity planning

resolution: Rolled back the CNI plugin configuration
